item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppDate 0.0.8: New Upstream
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: RcppDate ships the featureful date library written by Howard Hinnant to enable use from R packages. This header-only modern C++ library has been in pretty wide-spread use for a while now, and adds to C++11, C++14 and C++17 what is (with minor modifications) the ‘date’ library in C++20. The RcppDate package adds no extra R or C++ code and can therefore be a zero-cost dependency for any other project; yet a number of other projects decided to re-vendor it resulting in less-efficient duplication. Oh well. This release syncs with upstream release 3.0.6 made today. We also made another routine update to the continuous integration setup. The Debian and r2u packages for this new release have already been uploaded too.Changes in version 0.0.8 (2026-11-27)Updated to upstream version 3.0.6Regular update to continuous integration setup

item.title: Russell Coker: Coding Font Problems
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded:
Firstly here is how I would like fonts to work for coding.Coding requires monospaced fonts of a reasonably small size. To achieve that you need bitmap fonts. So a bunch of font creators design fonts that match their ideas of whatever is clearest to read. I select a font that is the product of a font designer who has similar ideas to mine about what is readable. Then my terminal emulator and other software fits the font glyphs of a size I select into an arrangement that exactly matches the bitmap size.That makes things easy for me and gives a result that’s as good as can be achieved. Font sizes varying by 0.1 point wouldn’t be an option because the font author didn’t write that many but that’s OK. I don’t want every possible size just the ones that can be displayed clearly.When you change the font size in points which is the only way most programs support changing the size the program will apparently fudge things with extra space or try to scale bitmap fonts and look ugly.Information on the DisplayThe command “” shows information on outputs which isn’t very useful for DPI but does show the scale factor (EG 1.5 for 150% scaling in display configuration).The command gives information on the real size and scaling via the fields width, height, logical_width, logical_height, physical_width, and physical_height fields. The scaling is width/logical_width. The actual DPI would either be “width/(physical_width to inches)” or “logical_width/(physical_width to inches)” which is the following on my laptop calculated with :$ qalc > 3840/(309mm to inches)
warning: Conversion of only part of an expression is not supported ("3840/(309mm" is converted to "inches)"). 3840 / (309 millimeters) ? 315.6504854 in^?1
> 2560/(309mm to inches)
warning: Conversion of only part of an expression is not supported ("2560/(309mm" is converted to "inches)"). 2560 / (309 millimeters) ? 210.4336570 in^?1This is not the DPI used for screen calculations. Firstly whatever the DPI is it will almost certainly be an integer to avoid using floating point maths as much as possible. Secondly DPI is mostly just made up anyway.According to the results of google searches (this Gnome Discourse discussion is one example [2]) increasing the “scale” to a non integer multiple (EG deciding to use 150% instead of 100% or 200%) causes the “scale” to be sent to the application as the smallest integer that is greater than the multiple used and the buffer that the application gives is then scaled down to the required size. So if you specify 150% (as I am doing on my laptop) then the “scale” number will be 2 and the application will give a double size buffer which is then scaled to 3/4 of it’s size. So 3840*2160 at 150% scaling means that a 5120*2880 buffer where things are rendered at twice the standard size which is then scaled back to 3/4 of it’s size.The way Wayland works for non-integer scaling (which is the common case for high-DPI laptop screens) significantly increases the memory use for application frame buffers (78% increase for 150%) and then requires another layer of scaling to convert those buffers to the resolution for display output. I thought that this was part of why my latest laptop with a i7-10610U CPU and 3840*2160 screen and 150% scaling feels slower than the previous one with i7-8550U CPU and 2560*1440 screen with 100% scaling.However recent updates to Wayland add a protocol wp_fractional_scale_manager_v1 for fractional scaling. It allows scaling in multiples of 1/120 of the screen size, presumably this number was chosen to allow 2/3 and 4/3 sizes to be handled cleanly. That protocol is served by the KWin Wayland system and used by Chrome and Kitty, it’s presumably used in most cases by KDE applications too. So the apps that I spend the most time using should all look great with fractional scaling and not take excessive RAM.As the “points” of font sizes are multiples of 1/72 of an inch and Wayland is deemed to have 96DPI that means the pixel height of a font on a 100% scaling system will be it’s “point” size multiplied by 96/72 which equals 4/3. In a test a system with 10.5 point Terminus font on Wayland with 100% scaling gave a distance of 16 pixels between the top of one letter and the top of the same letter on the line below. 10.5*4/3 == 14, so presumably there’s 2 pixels between lines in that case.For a system with fractional scaling and the Roboto Mono font I tested a system with 150% scaling and 9 point font which appeared to have 17 pixels from the top of a capital letter to the bottom of a lowercase p/q/g. 9*4/3*1.5==18 so in that case the font seems to have one pixel of space at the top or bottom. That case had 24 pixels from the top of one character to the top of the one on the next line so the vertical spacing seemed to be 6 pixels. On the same system with the Terminus font I found that it was 20 pixels from the top of one character to the top of the next line and 5 pixels space between the top of a capital and the bottom of a p/q implying a 2 pixel line spacing and 3 empty pixels at the top and bottom of characters.A scalable font gives the best clarity at arbitrary sizes. But for best clarity with the caveat of matching the pixel sizes a bitmap font is best.The following command shows the bitmap table in a TTF font file, no bitmap table means it’s a scalable font:ttx -l /usr/share/fonts/truetype/terminus/TerminusTTF-4.46.0.ttf|grep EBDTThe command is in the Debian package .The first command dumps the EBLC table (which has the bitmap sizes) to a XML file, it creates a file in the same directory so copy that file to /tmp or something first, the second file greps for bitmap sizes in the XML:ttx -t EBLC TerminusTTF-4.46.0.ttf grep ppem TerminusTTF-4.46.0.ttxFor Terminus this shows that all the bitmaps are square with sizes 12 14 16 18 20 22 24 28 32.The following command gives the point sizes that match the bitmap sizes for 150% scaling (the /1.5 in the equation):for n in $(grep ppemX TerminusTTF-4.46.0.ttx |cut -f2 -d\") ; do echo "scale=1;$n/4*3/1.5"|bc ; doneThe following kitty config disables the standard keys for increasing and decreasing font size and maps map ctrl+shift+equal kitten ~/bin/bitmap_size.py up map ctrl+shift+minus kitten ~/bin/bitmap_size.py downThe following is the ~/bin/bitmap_size.py script which was generated by ChatGPT and used the numbers generated by the shell commands from the previous section:from kittens.tui.handler import result_handler from kitty.fast_data_types import os_window_font_size
# font sizes in points = pixel_size * 72 / DPI (edit for your font and DPI) SIZES = [6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 14.0, 16.0]
def main(args): pass
@result_handler(no_ui=True) def handle_result(args, answer, target_window_id, boss): w = boss.window_id_map.get(target_window_id) if w is None: return cur = os_window_font_size(w.os_window_id) if args[1] == 'up': bigger = [s for s in SIZES if s > cur + 0.01] new = bigger[0] if bigger else SIZES[-1] else: smaller = [s for s in SIZES if s < cur - 0.01] new = smaller[-1] if smaller else SIZES[0] boss.change_font_size(False, None, new)The following shell script takes a TTF font file name as a parameter and gives a list of the point sizes needed to display at the natural sizes on the current Wayland display:#!/bin/bash set -e
LOG_WIDTH=$(wayland-info|grep logical_width:|cut -f1 -d,|sed -e "s/^.*: //") WIDTH=$(wayland-info|grep width|grep -v _width|cut -f2 -d:|cut -f2 -d\ ) MULT=$(echo "$WIDTH/$LOG_WIDTH"|bc -l)
if [ ! -f "$1" ]; then echo "usage $0 FONTFILE" exit 1 fi EBDT=$(ttx -l $1|grep EBDT 2> /dev/null || true) if [ "$EBDT" == "" ]; then echo "$1 is not a bitmap font" exit 1 fi TMP="/tmp/$(basename $1)" cp "$1" "$TMP" ttx -t EBLC "$TMP" 2> /dev/null TTX=$(echo "$TMP"|sed -e s/ttf/ttx/) A="" for n in $(grep ppemX "$TTX" |cut -f2 -d\") ; do A="$A, $(echo "scale=1;$n/4*3/1.5"|bc)" done OUT=$(echo "$A" | sed -e s/^,.//) echo $OUTThe following Kitty settings reduce the cell size to remove surrounding space:modify_font cell_height -2px modify_font cell_width -1pxA command like the following will display the style and postscript name of font files which can be useful when configuring a terminal emulator like Kitty which has text mode configuration for fonts.fc-scan --format "%{file} : %{style} : %{postscriptname} \n" /usr/share/fonts/truetype/robotomonoThe following commands are for selecting a font in the Kitty terminal emulator and then starting a new session displaying font choices to make sure it uses what you think it's using.kitten choose-fonts kitty --debug-font-fallbackOne problem I encountered while writing this post is the google "AI" that it gives as part of the default search page returning information that was correct but which was not easy to find in regular search results. This is bad performance by google and the result of using it is bad for society. Getting a LLM overview of a topic can be useful but when writing a document that's worth reading you can't include "trust me bro a LLM told me" you need an actual human source. The source can be documentation for a program that you don't use and while not great a forum discussion is adequate at this time. But eventually forums will start filling up with LLM generated answers and to continue this practice will end up with citing sites that have LLM output.

item.title: John Goerzen: A Long-Time Debian Developer Tries Modern NetBSD on a 1998 Alpha
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: Nearly 30 years ago, I purchased the most expensive computer I’ve ever bought: a brand new, 600MHz Alpha. I was quite excited about that thing: it was faster than any PC on the market, ran Debian quite well, and was fun to work with. Well, mostly. Finding a good browser was a challenge back then (Netscape wasn’t yet open source and they didn’t build for Linux on Alpha). Then AGP slots became popular shortly after buying it, so as a workstation its time was limited. As a server, though, I used it for about 15 years. So I guess my goal of investing in something high-end so it wouldn’t get obsolete so fast was mostly met.When it was time to pack it in, I took the guts out of it and reused the nice case for an x86 server. Now, as I’m setting up my vintage computer lab with the old equipment that had been in my attic, I thought it would be nice to reassemble the Alpha. I recently wrote about reassembling the hardware and restoring a tape backup from 2002 onto it, but I have another goal in mind: using it as a PPP server for my other machines to dial in to. Then I can use it to get onto Protoweb and BBSs with all the speed I tried for so many years to get past! Actually, this is a fun project.Performance-wise, the Alpha has a speed that sits somwhere in the range of a Raspberry Pi 2 or 3. But I’ve already got plenty of these, and only one Alpha. Reviving something on a platform that’s been dead for 20 years is going to be more of a challenge, and more fun, than setting up yet another Pi.So, out came the Alpha, the SYM53C875 SCSI card, the DEC Tulip card (with Linux drivers by Donald Becker), the Seagate Cheetah drive I added on shortly after I bought it. It all still worked, though the noise of the 10,000 RPM drive annoyed me even more now than it did then, so I used a newer IDE drive. (See my previous post for a recording of that Cheetah)The question now was: what operating system should I use? I always ran Debian before, and had long ago re-flashed the AlphaBIOS with the SRM BIOS, opening me up to non-Linux options also. While the Linux kernel still supports my 21164a CPU, Debian has long since dropped Alpha as an official platform, and so has just about everyone else in Linux-land, though it’s still alive and kicking. Gentoo technically still has an Alpha port, but it is permanently marked “testing” and outwardly appears to be moribund; the last post to the mailing list was a single message two years ago, and there have only been 6 posts this decade.I decided I would first try modern NetBSD, and later also opted to try modern Debian. The older Debian, which I restored in my earlier post, is still rock solid, but I wanted something with reasonable modern security since it will be exposed to the Internet. (And having something that speaks modern ssh will also be nice).Although I’ve been a Debian developer for 30 years, I have never been far from BSDs. My first *nix system, even before Linux, was FreeBSD back in the 90s. I’ve often had a FreeBSD system since (pfsense or OPNsense most commonly), and have used NetBSD as a workstation off and on also, plus I’ve had NetBSD in various VMs for quite some time. There’s a lot to like in NetBSD, and also some things that I found appalling.It is important for Free Software to have more than one Free OS. I am glad we have Linux, and I’m glad we have other OSs like FreeBSD and NetBSD. A monoculture is unhealthy, and we need different projects that do things in different ways and bring forth different ideas.So read both the praise, and the criticism, of NetBSD in that light. I am going to keep both NetBSD and Debian on this Alpha and likely use them both.My Alpha initially shipped with 256MB RAM. At some point in the past, I upgraded it to 512MB, which was its documented maximum, but was unable to get two of those sticks to work now. So my work started with it at 256MB, and I later managed to upgrade it to 1GB, its true maximum.I downloaded the ISO image and burned it to CD. I booted it on my Alpha’s IDE CD drive, and there was a lean, simple installation program. I partitioned the disk (SRM requires a BSD disklabel, so that worked out fine).Then when it came time to install the system, tar crashed. Every single time, tar crashed.It seemed to be related to the CD, though there were no errors in dmesg. I tried a network install, which worked, though the https option was unavailable and I was rather uncomfortable at the insecurity of doing the whole thing without TLS over the broad Internet. I rebooted and tried again from the CD; again no luck. I verified the burn of the CD matched the hash published on the site, and then served up the contents of the CD to the installer using a Linux machine on my LAN. That worked.The CMD646 has long been known to have some data corruption bugs. I remember that SCSI was always preferred on this board, and mostly used SCSI back in the day, but my old drives confirm using IDE CD drives with it without incident on Linux. The Linux driver certainly contained various workarounds back in the day, and may have done things like switch from DMA to PIO mode for CD drives. It’s possible the NetBSD driver lacks those workaround, though a post to the NetBSD Alpha mailing list suggests the problem may run deeper on NetBSD. In any case, calculating sha256sums of the data on the CD from within NetBSD produced incorrect results. The IDE hard drive, though, appeared to work OK.NetBSD initially reminded me of an old Unix in all the right ways. Clean, simple, seemed to run fine in the 256MB RAM the Alpha had at the time. My initial experience with NetBSD getty was nicer than I’d experienced with Debian’s agetty, though by the end I had ran into so many getty bugs that I had to to switch to mgetty.NetBSD vs. Debian on RAM usageThe top output is rather hard to parse; there’s nothing like the “available” column on Linux top/free, which basically shows how much RAM an application can use, considering both free RAM and caches that can be dropped. Before publishing this post, I did some comparisons to the modern Debian I installed on the Alpha. All of these tests were run at a time when 1GB of RAM was installed on the Alpha; some structures scale with physical RAM on both OSs. The test environment was NetBSD 11.1 and Debian sid (kernel 7.3).On a fresh install with sshd running and one active incoming ssh session, I observed this memory consumption (rounded to the nearest MB):Kernel RAM (static + dynamic): NetBSD 76 MB, Debian 88 MBUserland: NetBSD 46MB, Debian 22MBTotal: NetBSD 123MB, Debian 110MBIn short, fairly comparable. The Linux kernel is heavier by a few MB, while the Debian userland is lighter. This even though my Debian install wasn’t quite the minimal one; I added the ssh server and standard tools to it. I should point out here: yes, the Debian system is running systemd. Whatever you fault systemd for, heavy RAM usage doesn’t seem to be a problem.When looking at the installation process, Debian’s normal installer is less memory-efficient, as it loads more components into RAM, but there are ways to improve that (and alternative installation methods, which are routinely used on RAM-constrained systems such as Raspberry Pi). NetBSD’s installer becomes memory-efficient in part by ruthlessly excising every last thing it possibly can, including even TLS support.In the end, a default minimal install is quite memory-efficient on both. Debian runs well on my 512MB Raspberry Pis (as well as anything will on a system with that kind of CPU and microSD for storage), and doesn’t dip into swap there.Package management is hard to compare. On NetBSD, a lot of packages must be built from source, and that process is so resource-intensive that it completely blows past anything Debian does.The most favorable picture for NetBSD is working with the packages that are available as binaries. A “pkgin update” on NetBSD consumed 21MB at most, while on Debian, “apt-get update” used 61MB. On Debian, “apt-get install dar” rocketed through in a few seconds, completing the download and installation in less time than NetBSD took to complete the download (installation was similarly much slower on NetBSD). However, “/usr/bin/time -f %M pkgin install dar” on NetBSD reported max usage of 26MB, while “/usr/bin/time apt-get install dar” on Debian reported max usage of 120MB.This is not necessarily an entirely apples-to-apples comparison, however; Debian’s package system tracks all of the system (including what NetBSD calls the “base system”), has a larger pool to draw from, and generally has more features. pkgin on NetBSD is rather incomplete, especially on Alpha, and it therefore tracks far fewer packages. Bottom line: under extreme memory pressure, some basic package management functions are more memory-efficient, though slower, on NetBSD on Alpha, but I haven’t determined whether this is inherent or related to the size of the package database.However, as we’ll get into, the broader question of maintaining a system leads to considerably more RAM usage on NetBSD due to a need to compile from source.Filesystems and disk usageLinux has a fantastic smorgasbord of choices. You have the modern take on the traditional filesystem in ext4, ZFS is available, btrfs is there too, plus all the others like XFS, etc. At least two filesystems with lightweight checkpointing (ZFS and btrfs) are available.NetBSD supports ZFS, but with a lot of issues that you don’t see on FreeBSD or Linux with ZFS. Some of them are reminiscent of running ZFS on Linux maybe a decade ago. In any case, the Alpha doesn’t have enough RAM to run ZFS on any platform, so that’s out.NetBSD installed onto a UFS1 partition. This is an old-school filesystem like ext2. Somewhat to my surprise, although time_t is 64-bit on NetBSD, time_t on UFS1 is 32-bit. I discovered this when some C-Kermit tests were failing on the Alpha. There is also UFS2, which is somewhat newer (and has 64-bit time_t). But fundamentally these are still old-school fsck-type filesystems (though you can apparently enable a WAPBL log, it’s not enabled by default and I don’t know why).Disk usage-wise, a minimal NetBSD system used about 1.5GB compared to about 960MB for Debian (minimal system plus ssh server and system tools). Note that this involves installing some things like Python from pkgin for NetBSD, both because I needed it, and to make it more comparable to Debian.However, once pkgsrc is added, the NetBSD disk usage more than doubles, to 3.5GB due to the 292,000 files and directories it unpacks. Besides the obvious inefficiency of pkgsrc, NetBSD doesn’t split out development files into their own packages like Debian does, so packages that are only needed for their .so files wind up installing a bunch of .h and .a files also. You’re more likely to need these development files on NetBSD anyhow, due to the frequent need to compile packages from source. On Debian, you can install the -dev package if you want those, or leave it off if you don’t (as many people won’t). Nonetheless, we’re still talking sizes that, while on the higher side, are manageable on 30-year-old hardware here; I initially received that Alpha with a 9GB drive.To conclude, for resource efficiency: despite the general zeitgeist out there and the initial impressions, Debian has the lighter footprint. On a pure minimal system, this advantage isn’t all that significant. But it balloons once you start needing to install packages from source on NetBSD, which happens pretty quickly on Alpha at least.I don’t want to imply that there’s no bloat in a modern OS. These are both installations without GUIs, and a lot of bloat has happened in the GUI space. But I do want it to be clear that both of these OSs could easily run with 512MB of RAM or less, and have, and Debian at least is comfortable in under 2GB of disk space.I have an ADDS serial console built in 1983, and once I set up SRM to use it as its console, NetBSD picked that up automatically. No further setup was necessary other than just setting the TERM value in /etc/ttys, and even that wouldn’t have been necessary for most terminals (the ADDS is a pre-vt100/ANSI terminal). Nice!Debian fully supports serial terminals from SRM through its bootloader (aboot) and on into the system, but for the kernel boot process, console= must be passed on the kernel command line; it won’t auto-detect from SRM. Having said that, while the NetBSD kernel does support command-line parameters, its Alpha bootloader doesn’t support specifying them, so it’s fortunate it can inherit from SRM.I noticed that NetBSD would sometimes drop off the network. When I’d go turn on the serial console to see what had happened, of course there would be nothing there… and then everyhing was fine.Pretty soon, I realized that turning off the terminal attached to the serial console port caused NetBSD to drop the network connection. Further experimentation revealed the problem was actually deeper: turning off the screen caused NetBSD to hang, and turning it back on caused it to resume.After considerable head-scratching, I hypothesized that somehow NetBSD must be interpretying me turning off the serial terminal as a serial break. By default, this enters the kernel debugger, though I’d never know it, because the terminal is off. Nothing else happens when the kernel is in debug mode, and when I press Enter to show the login prompt, it exits the debugger.After running , I can now turn off my terminal without hanging the OS.This AlphaPC 164LX motherboard has two integrated DB-9 serial ports, both 16550A UARTs, which makes that part of it quite similar to a regular PC. But, alas, the first challenge is figuring out exactly what the serial port is named.That turns out to be a pretty big challenge. NetBSD continues to use a script named /dev/MAKEDEV like a traditional Unix. That means that your /dev probably has entries for a bunch of hardware you don’t have, and may lack entries for hardware you do have. dmesg lists com0 and com1, the com(4) manpage lists /dev/tty00 and /dev/dty00 as the devices to the first serial port, and there are also /dev/tty0 and /dev/dty0. Confusingly, all of those return an error when attempting to use them. Re-creating with MAKEDEV makes them a symlink, and that’s no better.I couldn’t find any reference guide anywhere to what serial ports are named on NetBSD. I finally just tried opening all of them, and fount /dev/ttyC0 and /dev/dtyC0 are the serial ports on my system. I have no idea why.Now, you’re noticing a dtyC0 and ttyC0. The dtyC0 is the “dialout”, and the tty is the “dial in”. Fine, but what’s the difference? This took me awhile to figure out. Apparently the tty devices block open() (unless passed O_NONBLOCK) until the remote end asserts CD (carrier detect) on the line. This is used by getty; put your modem into auto-answer mode, and rather than wait for CD to go high, getty just waits hours (or days) for open(2) to return. Different, but it works (in theory; as you’ll see, in practice, not so much.)I later added a 2-port PCI serial card. My on-motherboard ports moved from ttyC0 and ttyC1 (and dtyC0/dtyC1) to ttyC2/ttyC3. I guess it initializes the PCI cards first. That was a surprise, but fortunately the serial console just kept working anyhow, so that was nice.The pty subsystem on NetBSD has a condition in which it can silently drop data. I first noticed this while testing C-Kermit on NetBSD. A comment in /etc/sysctl.conf implies it is a long-standing issue for PPPoE as well. I can imagine it could also be a problem for things like ssh and telnet. I reported the kernel bug about a month ago, complete with reproduction code, but it’s had no activity at all. I verified it triggered on both x86_64 and Alpha, so it’s not Alpha-specific.I found two more pty bugs, both apparently due to race conditions in the kernel. I also reported 60993 and 61010 more than 2 weeks ago, and neither has had any activity yet.I confirmed on IRC that I was sending these reports to the right place, but they seem to not be getting any attention.I ran into quite a few issues bugs with the serial subsystem on NetBSD as well.The first was that getty doesn’t have a way to specify an init string for the modem. It turns out there’s an /etc/ttyaction file that can call a script, which if you use stty and chat carefully, can do this. This only works because ttyaction runs earlier than the manpage says (“The ttyaction file specifies site-specific commands to run when a login session begins and ends” isn’t correct; it’s run even before getty starts listening for a call on the modem.) It took a lot of experimentation to get right; whether or not to include clocal in the stty settings, for instance.To my pleasant surprise, getty on NetBSD has PPP auto-detection, and /etc/gettytab even had examples. This is nice, since it lets me dial-in without any login script for PPP, and yet still dial in with a regular terminal program to log in to the prompt.Unfortunately, it’s broken. More often than not, it failed to recognize PPP frames and tried to process them as a username, and sent back login prompts to the remote end. Needless to say, this didn’t work on either end. I had to disable it, and set up a user whose shell is /usr/sbin/pppd. That worked well enough.But I ran into two more serious problems: getty not noticing CD went high, and serial port lockup after CTS was dropped and then raised.By the time I was done with this on Alpha, I had tried three different serial ports for the modem: the built-in 16550A, a dual-port PCI expansion card with 16550As, and I even bought an old PCI USB card off eBay for the purpose of using with a FTDI USB-serial adapter. None worked reliably. I can’t be sure, but none of these issues seem to be Alpha-specific on NetBSD.Recall that the CD line going high is the modem’s signal to the OS that there is a remote modem connected, and that getty relies on open() blocking until CD goes high. Well, it turns out that sometimes open() never returns even after CD has been raised. This means NetBSD does nothing with the incoming call. It never reads anything and never sends anything, since getty is still waiting for open() to return. For the 16550 ports, at least, NetBSD allows me to open the dty port while getty is still waiting on the tty port, and by doing so, I was able to see that NetBSD did see the CD line going high. It just never returned at open(). The USB serial port didn’t let me open the device while getty was waiting, so I couldn’t verify there, but it seems like the same symptom.I was able to work around this problem by installing mgetty. I had used it on Linux back in the 90s when I ran a BBS, and I initially thought it wasn’t in NetBSD because pkgin didn’t find it. Turns out it was in pkgsrc, and this is what prompted me to install pkgsrc. All that for a simple C program.The other problem, with the serial port lockup, even mgetty couldn’t work around.With most “modern” modems, the modem maintains a constant speed on its serial interface to the computer (often 115200bps), while having a variable rate for its analog connection to the other end. This is because line conditions might cause handshaking at different speeds, and in-modem compression can cause transfer rates to exceed the raw bitrate. But you have to have a way to signal to a machine sending a lot of data to hold off for a bit, and then to continue. By far the best way to do this is RTS/CTS hardware handshaking. The modem signals to the computer to stop sending data by dropping the CTS line. When the modem’s small transmit buffer has been depleted, it raises CTS, allowing the computer to resume sending.When doing something like sending a file with ZModem, it is common to see the SD (sending data) and CS (clear to send; linked to the CTS line) lights go on and off in tandem.After initially getting dialin to work on NetBSD, I dialed in from a DOS box, then ran to connect to a BBS. However, whenever I tried to download a file using ZModem, the connection hung. Not just hung, but NetBSD was in a confused state and future logins were broken also.It turns out that when the modem dropped CTS, NetBSD stopped transmitting. But when the modem raised CTS again, NetBSD never got the message. It remained blocked on transmitting. Until, that is, some other event occurred on the line, such as receiving a character from the remote end. This apparently prompted it to check CTS and it got un-stuck.This explains why I didn’t see the problem with a PPP connection. With TCP, the download side sends ACK packets to confirm reception of TCP packets. Moreover, if no packets come in for awhile, it will timeout and send a packet. All of this combines to kickstart NetBSD’s CTS check and it seems to never have a problem there. The Kermit protocol, in its default configuration, also uses sliding windows with ACKs, so again, no problem there.ZModem, by default, is streaming. The receiving side sends nothing while the transfer is going on, so long as it’s receiving everything correctly. There’s nothing to cause NetBSD to unblock its writes.The only workaround for this one was to use hardware with a different driver. The USB FTDI interface didn’t have this problem, though I get frequent ohci “scheduling overrun” messages on my console from it. USB was not period-appropriate for this Alpha, though, so I’d rather not use it, and it still has the same open() issue.I’ve ordered a Prolific USB-serial adapter. I guess maybe that will work with both flow control and carrier detection, but at this point my NetBSD experiment has gotten rather expensive as I have to keep throwing different kinds of hardware at the software bugs.This is where things take a turn for the particularly disturbing.NetBSD has effectively two (or maybe three, depending on how you count) package systems: the base system (which unpacks tarballs) and pkgin/pkgsrc (pkgin installs binary packages, while pkgsrc builds from source).Updating these three sources are three different commands. (pkgsrc uses cvs update, which if any of you are old enough to remember CVS, should make you shudder.)There is a way to audit your installed packages for security vulnerabilities installed on your system. Not so for the base system. Note that the base system includes such things as ssh, SSL/TLS, curl, zlib, etc.The only way to find out when there are security bugs for the base system is to subscribe to both security-announce and netbsd-announce. security-announce seems to get a post once every 2 years, but when it does, it is important, though it doesn’t announce bugs fixed in the base system.NetBSD 11.1 became available recently, and it does indeed fix a number of security vulnerabilities. Unfortunately, you can’t just install a targeted set of packages. You have to reinstall it all, which takes a long time. So when there’s a security bug in brotli, or ssh, or whatever, you can’t just install a targeted patch. You wait for a new OS release and upgrade the whole thing (or, I guess, you could manually patch and rebuild, but this is impractically slow on Alpha). This looks untenable given the rate of security findings in 2026.As an example: NetBSD 11.1 came out on November 2. It was listed as fixing Brotli CVE-2026-111497 (published Oct. 22). Debian patched Brotli on Oct. 23, 10 days before NetBSD released 11.1. Debian’s patch would have been automatically installed by people running unattended-upgrades, and no reboot would be required (needsrestart would restart necessary daemons).There is nothing like unattended-upgrades for any of the systems on NetBSD.So, let’s say you want to get patches for security issues in the base system. To do that, you have to upgrade the base system.Upgrading the base systemThe standard manual tells you to boot the installation system again to install a NetBSD upgrade. Yes, that’s right. The standard instructions amount to burning a new ISO, booting from it, and installing the upgrade from there. Ouch. The NetBSD 11.1 announcement also suggests this method. (This is not an alpha-specific thing in the installation instructions; it’s also there for amd64).A different document also mentions a tool called sysupgrade to do this from a running system. sysupgrade isn’t part of the base system; it’s a package. But “pkgin install sysupgrade” doesn’t find it, so I have to build it from source. Another reason I had to install pkgsrc.Remember, to build even one package from source, you have to download a tarball containing the NetBSD packaging information for package. That’s a tarball with 290,334 entries, which took 22 minutes to extract on the Alpha.Then you “make” to build the packages you want. But oh, regular users don’t have permission, so yes, you’re running all the build tools as root. OK, you grit your teeth and run “make” and “make install” as root, and now you have sysupgrade!Sidebar: NetBSD installs the pkgsrc files owned by uid 600, gid 125, neither of which exist on the system. I’m not sure what the point of that is, and it’s not documented anywhere.So you can run “sysupgrade auto”, and it will download the base system tarballs and extract them. It will ask you about modifications to things in /etc. Most of them you have to tell it to keep your version; no, do not blow away changes to /etc/group, thankyouverymuch. I don’t know why it’s not smart enough to figure that out itself, since NetBSD 11.1 didn’t contain changes to the file anyway.It also asks about local changes to a bunch of files I never touched, such /etc/namedb/bind.keys and /etc/motd.Now at the very end of it, you see “sysupgrade: E: Some postinstall(8) checks have failed”. Oh joy. Hope you ran it in a terminal with scrollback.I found “postinstall checks failed: opensslcertsrehash” so I ran the script it told me to run, “sh /usr/sbin/postinstall -s /var/cache/sysupgrade/etc.tgz -d / fix opensslcertsrehash” and it seemed to be happy. Why it didn’t do that itself, I don’t know. I hope I didn’t miss any other failures.You can run “pkg_admin fetch-pkg-vulnerabilities” and then “pkg_admin audit”.On my Alpha, it shows quite a bit. Here are some excerpts: Package expat-2.8.2 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-66382 Package python313-3.13.14 has a command-injection vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-15366 Package python313-3.13.14 has a command-injection vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-15367 Package python313-3.13.14 has a input-validation vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-12781 Package python313-3.13.14 has a path-traversal vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-3479 Package lrzsz-0.12.20nb1 has a information-disclosure vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-10195 Package perl-5.42.2nb3 has a symlink-attack vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2011-4116 Package libxml2-2.15.1 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-8732 Package libxml2-2.15.1 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-0989 Package libxml2-2.15.1 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-0990 Package wget-1.25.0nb5 has a sensitive-information-disclosure vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-31879 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a command-injection vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16741 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a stack-overflow vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16742 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a stack-overflow vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16743 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a command-injection vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16744 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a stack-overflow vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16745 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-1010189 Package mgetty-1.1.37nb21 has a denial-of-service vulnerability, see https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-1010190But, after a fresh “pkgin update”, “pkgin upgrade” shows nothing to do.I checked a few of these. lzo and wget have nothing newer in NetBSD. libxml2 has a newer version available in pkgsrc, but it’s unclear if it fixes these issues.Python is annoying. You can’t just install python. You have to install a specific version. So there is now a python314 package; maybe it’s better? But python313 won’t auto-upgrade to it.I installed the python314 package, and now I have the same vulnerabilities in both. Sigh. They haven’t upgraded either the 3.13 or the 3.14 packages to the fixed versions.But look at mgetty. These bugs came out 7 or 8 years ago. The Linux distros that still shipped mgetty, including Debian, patched years ago when the vulnerabilities came out. A new upstream version has the fix. It would be for NetBSD to fix this. Clearly NetBSD is aware of the issues, since NetBSD’s own tools highlight it. In fact, if you are watching very carefully as you build it from pkgsrc, it will even print a warning about it — but it doesn’t pause for you to acknowledge, and had I installed it on anything with more modern speed, it’d have scrolled by before I’d ever noticed.You could make the case that NetBSD is an open source project, and it takes volunteers to fix things. You’d be right. But, back in July, I sent NetBSD a report about security bugs I’d found in C-Kermit, along with a patch to update their packages to a modern and fixed version (which, for the first time, runs NetBSD in CI), etc. I had understood the lack of progress on that one to possibly be impacted by extenuating circumstances; for instance, it’s a new major version from a new maintainer with a new Kermit project. A degree of caution is reasonable.Maybe I’m the first person to install mgetty for NetBSD for years. So perhaps you could say, “well, if I notice a bug, I could submit a fix.” But that makes the question be for me: do I have time in my life to spend so much time fighting bugs and security issues with NetBSD, or should I try a different OS or platform where the community is already taking care of such things?It certainly wasn’t the only reason, but it was this mgetty issue that pushed me over the edge to trying a modern Linux on this Alpha. Security needs to have less friction; when patching is easy, people will patch. NetBSD doesn’t make it easy in any respect, and keeping something in the system for 8 years despite knowing it has security issues looks really questionable to me.Conclusions and next stepsI’m going to keep NetBSD on this system. Partly because it is fun to play with something different, and NetBSD on an Alpha is most definitely different than what I’m used to. Partly because running an ancient version of Debian would be a security problem (yes I am aware that running DOS and OS/2 is also a security problem, but I’m managing that separately). And partly because, despite the complaints above, I really do enjoy NetBSD and have a lot of respect for what people are doing there. Having said that, this NetBSD box is pretty inefficient in terms of both time and money. Buggy serial system leads to needing to buy different hardware, and setting it up has taken a lot of time due to all these bugs, while maintaining it promises to take a lot of time also. Some of this is fun, but running pkg_audit, manually fixing things (or more likely, ignoring them), manually checking the base system for updates… that’s going to wear thin, and I’d rather play with my daughter than do that. Realistically, I don’t think I’ll keep up with it. At which point, well, maybe the ancient version of Debian doesn’t look so bad.But I’ve also tried modern Debian, and I’ll report on that in a separate post. Debian on Alpha isn’t without its quirks these days, either.I don’t know how long Alpha will be a viable platform. The lack of Rust and Go support for it is already a challenge, though there are efforts being made on both. As Debian and other parts of the Linux ecosystem rightly embrace Rust, that could further erode Alpha’s viability with Linux unless the Rust work reaches viability soon. Already some of my favorite programs (NNCP, Yggdrasil, and my own filespooler) would be a great fit for NetBSD, but are unusable on Alpha because of lack of Go and Rust support there. Perhaps gccrs will help in the future though. Still, I’ll enjoy the Alpha running an actual workload while I can!

item.title: Paulo Henrique de Lima Santana: My experience at Debian Reunion Brasil 2026
item.author: Paulo Henrique de Lima Santana
item.content:encoded: For some time, Daniel Lenharo and I had been considering organizing a meeting in São Paulo to bring the Debian community together for a few days. Unlike the MiniDebConfs that we host annually around April or May, this event would not feature talks, workshops, formal registration, sponsors, t-shirts, etc. Instead, the focus would be exclusively on hands-on contributions to the project - much like similar meetings held in other countries - bringing together Debian Developers (DDs), Debian Maintainers (DMs), and other contributors. We chose São Paulo to make it easier for interested individuals to attend, as the city is home to the country’s major airports, which would also help keep airfare costs more affordable.During DebConf26, held in July, we talked with other Brazilian contributors and decided to organize the first edition of Debian Reunion Brasil, taking advantage of a long weekend - coinciding with the national holiday for Black Consciousness Day - from November 20th to 22nd (Friday to Sunday). Additionally, David Tadokoro has secured a room at the CCSL (FLOSS Competence Center) at IME-USP.While at DebConf26, Daniel and I talked in person with the current Debian leader, Sruthi Chandran, and asked if Debian could provide financial support to cover travel expenses for contributors coming from outside São Paulo; she readily supported our request.Once the venue booking was confirmed, we began promoting our Debian Reunion to the community and inviting people interested in spending three days contributing to Debian.I traveled from Belo Horizonte to São Paulo on Thursday night (19th), and upon arriving at the hotel, I met up with the “curitibinhas” Daniel and Marcos Talau, and we went out to dinner. On Friday morning (20th), we met Thiago Pezzo at the hotel and headed together to the CCSL at USP. Once there, I ran into some other friends and met a few new people.We spent the morning discussing the organization of MiniDebConf Curitiba 2027, which will take place from April 25th to May 2nd. We covered the schedule of activities throughout the week, the venues, the sponsorship plan, bursaries, swag, and other details. It’s clear that meeting in person is far more productive than communicating remotely; I found our discussion very fruitful. There were 15 of us, and we all went to lunch together, which further helped us connect. In the afternoon, I took part in a planning session for the Debian Brazilian Portuguese translation team for 2027. I will continue to focus on keeping the translations for the debian.org website up to date, and I’ve committed to reaching out to and encouraging others to help translate .po files (for debconf, man pages, etc) ahead of the release of Forky in 2027. In the evening, I went to dinner with Daniel, Talau, and Thiago (along with his son), and we spent a great few hours chatting.On Saturday (21st), I dedicated my time to translating files from the debian.org website as well as various .po files. Lunch was, once again, quite enjoyable, and throughout the day - alongside our actual work - we frequently found ourselves discussing Debian, our events, the planning for our translation team, and so on. In the evening, while some headed out to enjoy the nightlife in São Paulo, Daniel and I went to grab some pizza near the hotel.On Sunday (22nd) morning, we headed to USP, and I took the opportunity to ask Charles a few questions about how to submit a package to proposed-updates. I needed to send a security fix for the python-engineio package to the stable distribution, It was my first time submitting a package to proposed-updates. Thanks for the help, Charles! I also took the chance to update the flask-socketio package to a new upstream version. We had lunch together again, and a few hours later, I left for the airport, as my flight back to Belo Horizonte was in the late afternoon. The return trip went smoothly, and I arrived home very happy to have taken part in the meeting.The CCSL rooms were perfect for hosting the Debian Reunion, and we discussed using the same venue next year, during the November 15th holiday. Let’s hope it works out and that we also have more people participating and contributing.Summary of my contributions over these three days:Reviewed of the work by the debian-l10n-ptbr team for the release of Debian Forky in 2027.New debian.org translations: portuguese/News/2026/20260831.wmlportuguese/News/2026/20260712.wmlportuguese/News/2026/20260807.wmlportuguese/releases/vote/2026/*001*Updated debian.org translations: portuguese/releases/index.wmlUpdated .po file translations: po://apt-listbugs/po/pt_BR.popo://dpkg/dselect/po/pt_BR.popo-debconf://zfs-linux/pt_BR.popo-debconf://openvox/pt_BR.popo-debconf://neutron-dynamic-routing/pt_BR.poThanks to Sruthi Chandran for accepting my request for financial support from Debian to cover my travel, accommodation, and meal expenses for attending the meeting.Thanks to Daniel Lenharo for his dedicated efforts in coordinating the organization of the meeting; without him, the event would not have taken place.Thanks to David Tadokoro, Rafael Passos, and Prof. Paulo Meirelles for arranging the venue and hosting us at USP.Thanks to all the contributors who took advantage of these three days to help improve Debian.

item.title: Vincent Bernat: Steering browser line breaks with invisible characters
item.author: Vincent Bernat
item.content:encoded: Let's benchmark with a short paragraph in French from Jules Verne's "L'Île mystérieuse":Le marin pressa la main du reporter, dont il ne pouvait se faire entendre, et d'une façon qui signifiait : « Attendez ! » puis, il rentra dans le couloir. Un instant après, il ressortait avec un fagot allumé, il le projetait dans les ténèbres, et il poussait des sifflements aigus.Let's try Firefox 160 first. The most notable "defect" for this paragraph is the word "": it may stay alone on the last line—or even be hyphenated. This is a "." With hyphenation disabled, are rarer, but the layout introduces "": a large blank space between the end of a line and the right margin, like in the second line when the paragraph width is 825 pixels. When the paragraph is justified, bad rags are translated into larger spaces between words. These traits make your text look poor and should be avoided.Like Firefox, WebKitGTK 2.54 may hyphenate "," leaving a very short on the last line. With and without justification, it often creates shorter paragraphs. When enabling both pretty wrapping and justification, WebKitGTK performs worse than any other browser in this example as it inserts too much space.My solution is to insert (U+00AD), except near the end of the paragraph, and to insert (U+00A0) to meet the minimal requirement to prevent a runt. In my case, I set the limit to 8 characters, punctuation included.The animation below marks each non-breaking space with a purple triangle and every soft hyphen with a vertical red line. With , the browser may insert a line break anywhere a soft hyphen is present.Such an approach cannot match a proper line-breaking algorithm, but it works in Firefox, prevents the shortened paragraphs in Safari, and sometimes provides better results than what Chromium did, as it allows hyphenation of "." Moreover, all browsers will break lines at the same places: with , each browser uses its own hyphenation dictionary and Safari ignores , while the specification for leaves the algorithm to each browser.I also add a bit of typographic sugar: I convert the straight single quotes and double quotes to their curly equivalents: and ; I turn an ellipsis into its dedicated equivalent ; I add a narrow non-breaking space before a double punctuation or between two groups of digits in French, like in "Ça fait donc 501 622 731."We could implement these transformations with regular expressions and a hyphenation library like Pyphen:However, it breaks if we have HTML tags in the middle:I have read "Dune".The naive regular expression transforms the quotes of the attribute. If we apply the regular expression to each text node, we get While we could tune the regular expressions, this approach is quite fragile. We need to apply the transformations to the plain text and stitch the HTML markup back into the result. I use the library to parse and manipulate HTML. Iterating over each block and extracting the text is straightforward, but we lose all the inner markup:Instead, we need to keep track of the position of each group of letters in a depth-first walk of the HTML tree. For example, we split the text from the previous HTML specimen into three slots:We translate modifications to the text into a list of substitutions: start position, end position, and new text.To apply a substitution, we locate the slot it applies to and update the text.We can stitch the modifications back into the HTML tree with a second depth-first walk, amending the text nodes when they are different from what we recorded in the slots.For this task, Python is not the fastest language on this side of the galaxy. But we can significantly speed up some parts of the code with Cython, a compiler to turn Python code into C extensions.I handle inline code a bit differently: I insert zero-width spaces before some markers: , , , , and . This lets the browser split a long IPv6 address, like 2a01:e0e:c03c:f44e:dabc:7337:38fa:ff40, or a Python method name, like xxhash.xxh3_128_hexdigest(), at those markers. As far as I know, this is not something possible with just CSS.When copying text, some browsers may keep the soft hyphens or zero-width spaces. This is annoying when pasting into a terminal. We can intercept the "copy" event and strip these special characters from the version recorded in the clipboard:Soft hyphens don't interfere with other features, like browsers' find-in-page or indexing by Pagefind.As with vertical rhythm, no one would notice this small arrangement if it weren't for this article. But, you know what? I notice it, and it makes me happy. So I'll keep spending time on pointless stuff like this because it soothes me. 🍃Maytham Alsudany reviewed a first draft of this article. Any errors are still mine!

item.title: John Goerzen: I Booted From My Tape Backup From 2002
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: Back in 2002, I had an Exabyte tape drive (7GB native / 14GB compressed) that ran Amanda and made backups of a few of my systems, primarily my Alpha system.To cut to the chase a bit, I managed to restore it and made the resulting environment bootable. Here it is, with KDE 2, Konqueror showing Internet of the time thanks to Protoweb, and Gopher showing a current Gopher server:This was a lot of fun and a bit of a challenge. Here’s the story.I had an AlphaPC 164LX with a 600MHz 21164a CPU. This is a bit of an intersting piece of hardware. It had the DEC Alpha processor, which was normally associated with more DEC-specific hardware. But the AlphaPC board tried to use the PC ecosystem. It had PCI and ISA slots, PS/2 keyboard and mouse, and was ATX form factor. The AlphaBIOS it shipped with could even boot a short-lived port of Windows NT to Alpha. I, however, primarily ran Linux on it.At some point, Linux started to strongly prefer the SRM text console, which was more designed for Digital’s UNIX and VMS OSs. I flashed that to the Alpha. Later on, I took all the guts out of the case and reused the case for an x86-64 server. But I still had all the parts.I put it all back together. Even my 10,000RPM UW-SCSI Cheetah drive still works, and still makes impressive and annoying noises. That recording was made when I installed it in an x86-64 to take an image from for preservation, before putting it back into the Alpha.But, that drive was from 2004, after I no longer used the Alpha as a workstation. It was mostly a headless server by then, and no longer as interesting.To get back to the workstation days, I needed to restore backups.In 2018, I sought to restore as much as I could from my Exabyte tapes before they degraded. My Exabyte drive had failed years ago, but I bought another on eBay. Combined with a SCSI card I still had, it wasn’t hard to read each file on those tapes onto files on disk. Most of the tapes read fine, though some had errors. That was step 1.The backups were made with Amanda, which is an orchestration layer over (mostly) tar. I had forgotten, but I had hacked Amanda back in the day to use bzip2 instead of gzip, to save some precious space on the tapes. So I had to replicate that hack, building a Docker container to do all this in, and modifying Amanda to read from the backup files I had created. I surmised that trying to do a bunch of testing on real tapes could risk degrading them further.After a whole bunch of hacking, I was able to restore a complete tree at each backup date (that didn’t depend on a tape with read errors). The data was safe, and that is where I left the project 8 years ago.I reassembled the Alpha from parts. After some initial issues with RAM compatibility, I got it all working.This is a photo of the Alpha. It’s the machine on the left. The one on the right is a more normal-sized tower. You can read more about the motherboard here.Rather than push my luck with hard drives that are about 30 years old now, I decided to use a BlueSCSI, which presents files on a SD card as SCSI devices to a SCSI controller. This made things much simpler, as I could put multiple disk images on there, and mount them on my laptop using the loopback device. All the while not worrying about damaging the fragile 68-pin SCSI connectors and moving actual drives from machine to machine.The boot disk on an Alpha must have a BSD disklabel partition table. This is because the bootloader is sought out at a specific spot on the disk that is designed to work around the precise location of a BSD disklabel. The bootloader then extends past that, so you usually create a partition starting after a gap, or make a sacrificial partition 1 that is designed to soak up the extra space needed by the bootloader (and you never put a filesystem on it). When booting from SRM, the Linux bootloader is called aboot. Lacking any way to install aboot from a modern system, I figured I would start from an existing Alpha disk image I had made, working with the partition sizes there (making a fresh filesystem as needed).This pretty much worked. I restored my backups, fixed up some permissions, edited some files like fstab and aboot.conf (roughly similar to grub.cfg), and booted.SRM started. aboot loaded! Yes! But the kernel promptly hung. There had been several kernel versions in that backup, and some of them hung and some didn’t.I had already tried booting a newer system from those saved hard disks, so I knew that the kernel could boot. It just wasn’t. I remembered I had probably built my own kernel back in the day, and theorized that I had probably built it to only be booted from AlphaBIOS and its MILO boot loader. I copied a generic Debian kernel from one of those hard drives to it, and now it booted!I couldn’t remember what video card had been in that system. From reading the /var/log/XFree86.0.log file, I concluded it was a Permedia 2 card that I had put into my K6-3/400 OS/2 system. Oops. I had bought a FireGL 1000 clone for the alpha, and after a few battles with XFree86 and broken acceleration, got X to run with it.KDE’s taskbar, then called Kicker, wasn’t working. It segfaulted almost immediately. Apparently I had added one of these CPU or disk monitors to it, and that thing had a bug with parsing the structures in whatever kernel I had. Editing some config files removed that monitor and then Kicker worked.At this point, everything from the Alpha seems to work except Netscape Communicator. Netscape never released a version for Alpha on Linux, but they did for Alpha on OSF/1. My backup still had the necessary OSF/1 compatibility libraries. Unfortunately, Debian’s generic kernel didn’t compile in OSF/1 support. I haven’t yet taken the step to do so myself. But, I also used Konqueror from KDE off and on over the years, and that was working.I ran mutt, and there it was: my INBOX just as it was when it got backed up in summer of 2002. My UUCP configuration was still present. Some files from running a build daemon for Debian were there. So there you have it. A snapshot of 24 years ago. It still had Kermit on it, which back then I mostly used to talk to my HP 48GX calculator. But even C-Kermit 7 from 2000 still talks perfectly to modern C-Kermit 11 and that was the quickest way initially to exchange files. (ssh and SSL have changed a lot since then.)It’s fun exploring my files from back then. Although I took care to migrate data to new machines when I got them, it’s different to see them all in their original context and what I was working on back then, or to use the up arrow and see what was in my bash history.I’ve also worked to install modern NetBSD and Debian Linux on this. More on those projects in future posts.

item.title: Maytham Alsudany: Relicensing the entire Debian wiki (part 1)
item.author: Maytham Alsudany
item.content:encoded:
So the Debian wiki's been around for 25 years, but no-one thought about licensing when it was started. There have been a few short email threads over the years on this topic, but nothing actually happened. Now, since gears are turning on moving the wiki to MediaWiki, we're finally trying to fix the licensing issue... yay us! The wiki started in 2001 running under wiki.debian.net, which used a custom licence with the bare legal minimum to allow content to go on the wiki. As you can probably tell, this is not a "free" licence with respect to the Debian Free Software Guidelines.For those who don't know, the Debian Free Software Guidelines (DFSG) define whether a given piece of software (or in this case, adapted to writing and media works) is "free" as in freedom. You may be more familiar with the Open Source Definition, which was adapted from the DFSG.In 2005, wiki.debian.org was established running MoinMoin, the software that it still uses today, and content was imported from wiki.debian.net. At this time, Jonathan Dowland raised concerns on the lack of licensing terms on the new MoinMoin installation as well as the copyright status of the content being imported, but it happened anyway. As he puts it, "the question is now whether the material on this site is DFSG at all and if it ever will be." Currently, the Debian wiki is the biggest wiki on the internet that uses MoinMoin according to Steve McIntyre during DebConf25.Yet, there was no clear licence for the content people were putting on the wiki. And when there is no licence, and no-one specifies a licence on the page itself, it is assumed to be "all rights reserved" in most jurisdictions. This is ignoring the implicit grant given by an editor to display that content on the wiki when they submit content to the wiki, but this is shaky at best and doesn't provide the clear permissions needed to freely reuse that content.Steve McIntyre hosted a Debian Wiki BoF (Birds of a Feather meeting) at DebConf 25. During DebConf 25, there was a BoF meeting to discuss the wiki, preceded by a great "biased SWOT analysis" presentation by the Arch Wiki admins on how they run their wiki and the challenges they faced. The wiki BoF discussed a range of topics, one of which was licensing.At the same time, I started pushing to fix content licensing, and for the last 16 months, I have been largely working alone to slowly but surely relicense everything ever put on the wiki. This article aims to document what has been done so far and why, and some challenges encountered along the way.You can watch the wiki BoF: low quality, HD (warning: choppy audio), and the Arch Wiki presentation: low quality, HD, thanks to the DebConf Video Team who recorded them during DebConf 25.It is designed explicitly for content and media, compared to other licences that are aimed at software (e.g. MIT).It requires attribution for contributors' hard work.It ensures any adaptations of the work continue to use the same or compatible licence, preventing someone from taking the work and making it proprietary.It is pretty permissive and allows adapting CC BY-SA 4.0 materials into GPL-3-licensed works, like package manual pages and other documentation.Some licences were ruled out for various reasons: - We wanted a licence that required attribution, especially considering the wiki relies on volunteers to populate and update its content.This would also make it difficult for any content to be brought into the wiki from other sources, since they would have attribution requirements that could not be preserved under CC0.GNU Free Documentation Licence (GFDL) - Debian only considers the GFDL to be a DFSG-free licence when it is used without any of its invariant options as per the 2006 general resolution. Also, this licence would limit where wiki content could be integrated outside of the wiki. Generally, this is an unwieldy licence with many restrictions, and should probably be reserved for printed works as it was designed for that.Creative Commons NC & ND options - The Non-Commercial (NC) and Non-Derivative (ND) options for Creative Commons licences are not compatible with the DFSG.It's not like CC BY-SA 4.0 is a niche licence; it is the licence that Wikipedia uses. As a result, we can copy content back and forth from a whole lot of places with this licence.Overall, CC BY-SA 4.0 provides a balance between putting in place protections for the work contributors put into the wiki via requiring attribution and share-alike, while also being very permissive in every other aspect, in line with the kind of freedom we're looking for.The Debian Wiki displayed a prominent banner regarding the licence of new content.Before dealing with the mess that is the old content, first we looked at how to handle new edits to the wiki.After picking an arbitrary future date (in this case, 24 July 2025), I wrote a new copyright page explaining that content contributed after this date would be licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, and summarised the main points of the licence.Following this, I updated the website footer and added a banner notifying wiki users and editors of the licence change (or should we say: addition). It was ugly, prominent, and in to make sure no-one missed it. The banner served its purpose for a few months, and then was removed because, by then, we're pretty sure we got the message across.I also ensured this was displayed properly on the 'edit' page, so that editors understood that, by submitting their changes to the wiki after this date, they agreed to license their contribution under CC BY-SA 4.0.Now, to the annoying part. In order to actually get everything to use CC BY-SA 4.0, contributors need to be contacted one by one and asked for permission to relicense their work, as they are the copyright holders.Keep in mind that the end goal is for all content on the wiki to be DFSG-free, with CC BY-SA 4.0 being the preference.Wait, how much work is this?Allow me to first give you an idea of the scale of the task at hand:There are 21,506 registered user accounts on the wiki .Over have been made to the wiki.Of those user accounts, 9,778 users have made one or more edits on the wiki.Only 1,548 users have made more than 20 edits on the wiki.These numbers are based on a snapshot from 26 January 2026.For that last bullet point, this graph here makes it clear that the majority of user accounts (on the left side of the graph) have only made a handful of edits. Frequency of number of edits per contributor. Each point shows how many contributors made a given number of edits. The horizontal axis uses a logarithmic scale.Though unrelated to the topic at hand, this is probably a good argument for allowing anonymous edits to the wiki once again, a setting that was originally disabled to reduce spam. New accounts requiring manual approval, which has been in place for the past few years, was put in place for the same reason as well.These kinds of protections mean wiki admins have to deal with less spam, but they also increase friction, which makes it harder for readers to make one-off edits and should be minimised as much as possible in the opinion of Weird Gloop, the folks behind a bunch of notable wikis, like the Minecraft wiki. Hopefully the move to MediaWiki will greatly improve the anti-spam tools available to allow for this to happen.At the moment, what I've been doing is checking pages one at a time to determine who needs to be contacted, and emailing them. While I've been doing this, I have kept an evolving record of who has been contacted, who has agreed, and who cannot/will not agree in a Git repo on Salsa (Debian's GitLab instance).The first thing I did was write a small script that listed pages that were three or fewer clicks away from the front page. This way, I could start with the important pages first. This turned out to be very annoying to work with, as these pages also had the most edits and unique authors (who could've guessed?). Many of them were "portal" pages as well, which are big collections of links rather than real content, so I tended to skip these.I've created a little bit of JavaScript that acts as a bookmarklet (i.e. button in the bookmark bar that does things rather than open a URL). What it does is highlight usernames on the edit log of a given wiki page (which MoinMoin calls the "Info" tab) based on a colour code: green means agreed, yellow means contacted with no response yet, and red means "failed". This gives a great overview of the status of each contributor to the page, and also filters out edits made after the 24 July 2025 cut-off.The bookmarklet script highlights the username associated with each revision to show the relicensing status of each contributor.Many pages have been completely rewritten or transformed so much that none of the original remained, so there was no point in contacting every contributor in the edit log if I could determine only the ones that mattered. Additionally, if all someone did was fix a typo or grammar mistake, they were also not worth contacting (though this was usually decided on a case-by-case basis).This introduced a new problem; how can I filter out these contributors to find the editors responsible for the current content? The first thing that came to mind was . So naturally, I ran a script on the Debian Wiki server overnight to transform the MoinMoin data into a giant Git repo, where each commit represented an edit, and the author was set to the editor's username and account email address. This resulted in a 252 megabyte repo with 290,052 commits.MoinMoin stores its data on the filesystem, rather than a database like MediaWiki does. The data directory contains a directory and directory.Each page is represented as a directory under , with special characters in page names encoded in a Moin-specific format. For instance, the page DebianDeveloper/Benefits is stored under pages/DebianDeveloper(2f)Benefits/.Within each page, there is a directory (which we don't care about), a directory containing a copy of the page at each revision (e.g. ), a file containing the number of the latest revision, and an file containing the edit history of the page in tab-separated values (TSV) format.The file stores the timestamp, revision number, username, IP address, and user ID for each revision, so using this and the data in the directory, a Git repo could easily be constructed with a bit of scripting.The final step was adding the user's email to the commit, which made it easy to associate usernames with emails within the Git repo. Each user has a file in the directory named based on their user ID (assigned by Moin), and one of the attributes contained in that file is the user's email address.Overall, the file tree looked something like this:. ├── pages/ │ └── <page name>/ │ ├── cache/ │ ├── revisions/ │ │ ├── 00000001 │ │ └── 00000002 │ ├── current │ └── edit-log └── user/ └── <user id>Now I could a page and find out exactly who should really be contacted, making this process much faster than reviewing every revision of a page by hand. This wasn't a foolproof method though, as it would blame a user for an entire line for both additions and modifications, like rephrasing a sentence or fixing a typo. It was a good starting point though, better than contacting anyone that ever edited the page. Additionally, tended to be really slow, taking a few minutes every time it was run, likely because of the amount of commits involved.I also made a wrapper around to highlight lines in green, yellow, and red, allowing me to identify which lines remained to be reviewed. The colours mean the same thing as before with the bookmarklet script.The wrapper script produced a coloured output to determine the status of each editor of the page.Recently, rather than using that 3-clicks-or-away list of pages to review, I have been sporadically reviewing any pages I stumble upon while doing other work. It may be less efficient, but it's more fun and feels less like a chore compared to reviewing pages one after another.Of course now we need to do the most important part, actually contacting people over email.For each user, the starting point is to retrieve the email address they have on their wiki account. Luckily, since I've got the repo as a git repo, I can git log -1 --author=<username> to do this rather than ping the wiki data each time.Now there were a few problems with this:Email addresses were only verified for new accounts. This meant that some users changed the email address on their account to an invalid one, often intentionally (instead of asking for their account to be deleted).Some email addresses were outdated and no longer existed. The most common case was for addresses for people who have left the Debian project.This meant that a little internet detective work was needed for some users, which involved checking things like searching Debian New Members and mailing lists. Sometimes users had a user page on the wiki with better contact info as well.If I'm able to find a working email address, then I send them an email based on a template, which has been refined a couple times. It pretty much summarises what's going on and asks for permission to relicense their work to CC BY-SA 4.0.These emails were sent from my address, mostly relying on its domain reputation to cut through spam filters and end up in people's inboxes. I also CC'ed myself at a special address, which allowed me to filter relicensing stuff into its own folder. Though, people kept leaving it out of their replies, so I ended up changing the filter to check the email subject instead. Eventually, I plan to create a Git repo containing an per user to keep a record of people's responses.Most failures occurred because the email address could not be found or the recipient mailserver had an issue, so I'd get that "Undelivered Mail Returned to Sender" email. In these cases, I wasn't able to find an alternative address. Other failures were mostly due to the contributor having passed away, and only one person so far has actually refused to relicense their work among those who have responded to the emails. All of these are being collectively referred to as "failed" users with regards to content relicensing.At the time of writing (25 November 2026), the progress is as follows: users have been . (47%) users have their work.The remaining have yet. users have been put down as .This is pretty good progress: of the 1,548 users who made 20 or more edits, 51% have been contacted, 24% have agreed to relicense, and only 4% have been marked as failed.Of course, not every contributor has been contacted yet, there are many more to go.It would be great if there was a way to automate this, as a lot of it is repetitive. has worked so far, but its limitations mean it still requires human review. Ideally, there should be a way to find the authors of the latest revision of the page based on word-diff rather than line-diff, and also rank them based on how much they contributed to the page. Maybe it would involve measuring Levenshtein distance per edit? Who knows?At the moment, I don't have time to work on such a tool. So I'll keep doing it the same way I've been doing it so far: every once in a while when I open some page on the wiki, I will check who is yet to be contacted, and send out a handful of emails.This likely entails stripping out each failed user's contributions from the wiki wherever it is part of the latest revision, which can also mean that some pages will need to be completely deleted as well. This is not a good thing, but it's something that has to be done to reach the aforementioned goal of a completely DFSG-free wiki.This kind of thing probably should wait until the move to MediaWiki has happened. The tooling for doing these kinds of mass edits is much better there, and I think(?) there are plans to create a static archive of the MoinMoin wiki during or after the move, so that information isn't lost forever. This would be part of the general effort to clean up the wiki.Following up when there is no responseA lot of the people who have been sent emails have not responded in a long time (>3 months, many much longer than that). These people need to have follow-ups sent to them, since there is a high chance the email ended up in their spam folders. I have sent follow-ups to a few people, some of which have succeeded, but this needs to be done in bulk for all the remaining people.A limit also needs to be put in place before we give up on people. One approach would be to mark users as failed if they do not respond to two further follow-ups after the initial email, each spaced at least a month apart from the previous email, for a total of at least three months from first contact. This would be loosely based on the kind of procedure used by the Debian MIA Team.A while ago, I floated the idea on the wiki mailing list of asking the Publicity Team to create a Bits post (for instance) to let everybody know about the relicensing effort, and to ask contributors who have not been contacted yet to send an email. This proactive approach would be much better and less work than the current reactive approach, since asking every person to send one email is a whole lot easier than one person sending hundreds of emails. Even though little interest was shown on the mailing list at the time, at some point, I'd like to follow through with this.In a way, this post is serving the same purpose! You probably didn't know about what I'm doing before reading this, but now you do :)Have you ever, before 24 July 2025, edited the Debian wiki? Well step right up! It'd be great if you could send me a short email with the following format:To: maytham-wiki-license [AT] debian (DOT) org Subject: Relicensing my contributions to wiki.debian.org
Hi,
My username on wiki.debian.org is <INSERT USERNAME HERE>.
I give permission for all work I have submitted to wiki.debian.org to be distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license, the text of which can be found at https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/.It means I don't have to chase you down, which is great! Also note that the address will be checked to make sure it's genuine, and it would be even better if you could GPG sign it!Now for the complicated bit: Debian being a volunteer project is both a blessing and a curse. Having more people help out with this work would make this initiative much more sustainable. As someone put it in an email to me: "I am concerned about the bus factor of one Maytham." This is especially important as I've recently slowed down my work on this due to other matters that are either more important or just plainly more interesting.If you want to help with contacting people, there is a short guide in the repo README. In short, find the contributors you want to contact (and make sure they have not already been contacted!) and send each of them an email based on the template, CC'ing my licensing email address so that it gets saved in my mailbox for the future export. Then, you can modify the lists to add users to contacted, succeeded, etc.Hopefully with a bit more work, we can get this across the finish line. This article is part 1 because the work is unfinished and still ongoing, so hopefully the progress numbers will be higher in a potential part 2 to the saga.
