item.title: Sergio Cipriano: My experience at Debian Brazil Reunion 2026 in São Paulo
item.author: Sérgio de Almeida Cipriano Júnior
item.content:encoded: Last weekend, I attended the first Debian Brazil Reunion.Inspired by similar events organized in other countries, we decided to bring the idea to Brazil and organize a three-day event focused on contributing to Debian.Every day, we started at 9 a.m. and worked until around 8 p.m.I was so immersed in the event that even after getting back to the hotel, I kept working. I was having so much fun that I just couldn't get out of the mood of getting things done.What everyone was working oneA few people were working on translations into Brazilian Portuguese, another group was organizing the MiniDebConf that will take place in Curitiba next year, and the rest of us, myself included, were working on packaging and other development-related tasks.One thing that made me particularly proud was seeing Lucas Ramalho and Giovanna Macedo travel all the way from João Pessoa to attend the event.I first met them a few months ago during Debian Day, when I went to João Pessoa to give a packaging workshop and a talk about what it's like to be a Debian contributor.Seeing them again in São Paulo, eager to learn more about packaging, really inspired me to keep helping newcomers.It's normal for people to come and go when making their first contributions. That's why it's always rewarding to help someone and see them stick around and become part of the project.I managed to upload neovim-promise-async, a package that ships both a Neovim plugin and a Lua library.It was my first time packaging a Lua library, so I learned a lot by reading the dh-lua code to better understand a few details of the Lua ecosystem. Writing dh-lua.conf was a bit confusing at first, but it turned out to be simpler than I expected. I also had fun coming up with an autopkgtest for the package.During the MiniDebConf Brazil, Antonio Terceiro gave a lightning talk about salsa-scripts, a tool he developed to help him approve Salsa accounts without having to use the GitLab interface.I really liked the idea, but there was one limitation: only members of the salsa-admins team could use the tool. I tried to join the team to help with account approvals, but the only way to do so was by having an account with full administrative privileges.I don't want that, and I agree with them that people should not have that level of access just to help approve new accounts.My goal was to solve the problem of approving accounts during workshops. I hate having to pull commits from GitHub just because someone hasn't had their Salsa account approved yet. And I'm not blaming the salsa-admins team. It's simply impossible to approve accounts quickly enough to keep up with the pace of live events.That's when I came up with the idea of adding a feature to salsa-scripts that would allow any Debian Developer to approve new accounts.I shared this idea Aquila, and he introduced me to Debian Gitlab self-service. I wasn't aware of this project, and after discussing it, we decided that implementing the feature there would make more sense than adding it to salsa-scripts.Aquila took the idea I had been putting off for a while, implemented the whole thing in just one day, and the result turned out pretty cool:Finally, I also sponsored a few uploads. I helped Tobias Sette and Giovanna Macedo with their first uploads to Debian.It's always nice to help newcomers in person. It's much easier to explain things in detail, answer questions as they come up, and get things done faster than going back and forth reviewing merge requests.It was an amazing experience!I want to thank Rafael Passos and David Tadokoro for making this happen. They managed to reserve one of the classrooms at the University of São Paulo (USP). Without that, the event would have been much more expensive if we had needed to rent a coworking space.It was also my first time visiting USP, which was a nice experience. It's one of the most important universities in Brazil!I'm already looking forward to the next edition!

item.title: Michel Lind: Hello (again) Debian!
item.author: Michel Lind
item.content:encoded: As of 2026-11-24 I became a Debian Developer, uploading! This has been a long time coming - I became a Debian Maintainer all the way back on 2022-08-24, 4 years and 3 months ago - work not being a Debian shop (though you never know what the future holds), it has been slower getting to a point when my portfolio of packages is varied enough that I feel confident applying.It is even a longer time coming if one considers that I have been thinking of becoming a Debian developer since… 1998! At the time transportation was more of an issue though, and VCs were not really a thing, so it can be hard… to get the key endorsement I needed.Everyone has been very supportive - going chronologically, thanks to who advocated my DM application, and for all the advice in #debian-mentors, for enticing me to dabble with updating which involves learning about minutiae - and of course, my Application Manager, who patiently shepherded my application, and for all the pointers on procedures throughout.And my ex-colleague Phil Dibowitz, author of sugarjar, who persistently (but nicely) asked why this package is still not in testing (because it has broken dependencies) to the point I figured out I should stop delaying, get my DD on, and then I don’t have to beg DDs to sponsor NMU uploads ;)It’s also a nice sabbatical present - I’ve been due one since October, and after a year full of dealing with CVEs at work and trans-Atlantic relocation - we finally moved to what is hopefully our forever home - it was serendipitous that the keyring update actually happens the first day I am on leave! (I must confess I still had the work laptop open in the morning, since there are files I need to dabble with open source projects I did not get transferred the day before).So… what will I be doing? I have some Debian packages due, including a new package and an NMU update I worked on during my DD application. Now that work pressure is abated temporarily, I also plan to strengthen my artisanal coding muscles by starting a long-delayed Fennel project, and learn Zig for advent of code…Expect normal service to resume in January, hopefully with a refreshed and less grumpy Michel.

item.title: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey: The Bub's Brothers: a 21 year old ITP comes back to play
item.author: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey
item.content:encoded: «Great to see that someone is trying to make that old project survive!» — Armin Rigo, author of The Bub’s Brothers, 2026«Something I wasn’t expecting to ever hear about again, TBH. Good to hear.» — David Gowers, who redrew its graphics in 2007 — Alex Myczko, Debian Developer, 2026, after the first game over the Internet in yearsChapter 1: A Mac game, cloned for the network (2003)In November 1997 Sebastian Wegner, known as McSebi, released for the Mac as shareware, his own take on Taito’s arcade classic Bubble Bobble. Two dragons, bubbles, monsters trapped inside them, fruit everywhere.On 31 January 2003 Armin Rigo, one of the founders of PyPy, made the first commit of a network clone of McSebi’s game, written in Python. The old site said it plainly: «This version is a direct clone of the MacOS game Bub & Bob of McSebi», and thanked him: «Thanks Sebi for all the cool graphics and sounds!»It didn’t stay a one-man project for long. Gio, Odie, Michel-Stéphane and Armin wrote levels in Python, paxed improved the random levels, and David Gowers redrew the graphics in 2007. And in 2005 McSebi did something that turned out to matter a lot: he put his graphics and sounds under the Artistic License.The last commit is from 12 October 2013. Then silence.Chapter 2: Ten years in Debian (2005 to 2019)In 2005 a Debian Developer filed an ITP, an “Intent To Package”, for the game (#308148). It reached the archive in February 2008, and for more than ten years got you a LAN party in one command.Around 2008, in Debian: a ten-player game over the network. Look for tarzeau on the scoreboard: that’s Alex. Screenshot: screenshots.debian.net.Then Python 2 reached its end. In October 2018 someone asked for a move to python3-pygame (#912480). Nobody did it. On 30 September 2019 the game left Debian, and the removal bug says why in four words: «python2 removal; dead upstream» (#936248).Chapter 3: A Debian Developer with a long memory (2026)That Debian Developer was Alex Myczko, and he never forgot the game. In 2021 he imported it from SourceForge into his own GitHub repository, and in 2024 Christopher Bock sent a first automatic conversion to Python 3. Then, in 2026, I wrote my first post on Planet Debian, about rescuing old software. Alex read it, got in touch, and asked if I fancied porting the game to Python 3.Of course I did. Bringing old games and software back is what I enjoy most. I spent 20 years tracking down the authors of Conquer, a 1987 Unix game, until it became free software, and I adopted xwpe, a 1993 programming editor. A game people loved, thrown out only because the language under it moved on? That’s my kind of project.At some point I asked him on GitHub whether that 2005 ITP was his. His answer: .«python2 removal; dead upstream».Chapter 4: Bringing it back (2026)Alex reviewed and merged everything in his repository and tagged the releases, 2.0 up to 2.3. Along the way anzz1 joined in with a lot of fixes, from sharper scaling to releasing the keys after a rewind. Most of the port was the usual Python 2 to 3 work. A few problems were properly fun, though.One bonus is a clock that rewinds the game. On Python 2 it relied on , a C module whose own comment brags «This one can copy running generators and their frames!». It did exactly that, poking straight into CPython’s frame structures:There’s no way to port that. Those structures are private and change with every Python release, and PyPy can’t copy generators either. Without the module the game just printed «‘statesaver’ module not compiled, no clock bonus».So now the game simply plays the past again. When a board starts it saves a checkpoint of plain data: players, dragons, monsters, bonus state, and the state of the three random generators it uses. Every input from the network (keys, players joining or leaving) is logged with the pass number it arrived in. To rewind, the game rebuilds the board from the checkpoint and runs it forward again, with the sound off, up to the moment you land on.That only works if the game is fully deterministic, so there’s a test for it. It runs a server with two scripted players and hashes the screen and the game state after every pass. Two runs with different values must give identical hashes. A rewind recomputes 1,644 passes, and the 602 passes that follow must match a run that never went back. (commit)The network protocol glued message codes, which were , onto output. Python 3 says no to that, so the server died building the very first icon. Now everything on the wire is , and raises if you hand it a instead of guessing an encoding:Then there’s division. I walked the syntax tree for every in the code, 82 of them, and 13 divided two ints and needed . One of them, , blew up only when you loaded a level without wind. The nice part: the protocol didn’t change, so a Python 2 client still plays against a Python 3 server, and the other way round. (commit)To join a game you click a dragon. Alex tried it on Wayland and wrote: «i saw graphics, heard music, but no input worked». The GTK client read the mouse on the top-level window. With client-side decorations, the window’s coordinates include the title bar and the shadow, so on GNOME, KDE and Weston every click landed 26 pixels to the right and 60 lower. The dragons sit at the bottom of the screen, so your click landed below the playfield and nobody could join. The fix was to read the mouse on the drawing area instead:The client picked the first display driver that loaded, and X11 was first in the list, even with no X server around. Now X11 goes last. Full screen asked for a 656x400 video mode, and Wayland compositors never let an app change the mode: Sway left it in a window, others drew a tiny playfield in a corner. pygame 2’s flag fixed full screen. For a resized or maximized window the game now scales the picture itself, keeping the proportions.To stop this from breaking again there are display tests with real input: X11, Weston, Sway, KDE and GNOME, each in its own headless session. Most of them get input from . One gotcha: you must not pass , because then the events are synthetic, and Weston’s X11 backend throws those away. GNOME has no X input at all, so there the test drives the mouse through Mutter’s RemoteDesktop interface over D-Bus. Each test clicks a dragon, presses keys, and checks that the game saw them and that the picture fills the window. With the old code, the GTK client fails on Weston, KDE and GNOME. (commit)Then Alex wrote from Hyprland: «fullscreen works now. and also input works (i only had completely forgotten how it works, clicking dragon, then keys for left/right/jump/bubble :) we should setup an internet server, and have some fun»The public list of games used to live on codespeak.net, the server from the early PyPy days, which is long gone. The game could hang or spit errors trying to reach it. Now the server is a setting, and there’s a systemd unit to run your own. Alex set one up at bubble.aiei.ch, then wrote , and: «@vejeta what about you join?» So I joined, and we played over the Internet, 13 years after the last commit.The Internet server list is back, on Alex’s meta-server. I blurred the server’s address.Debian wants to know the licence of every file, and the game has seven subgames, each with its own tune. Nobody knew where those tunes came from. The old CVS log named just one: The others only said things like I compared them against a big pile of game soundtracks and module music, and all I learned was that each tune sounds like the game its subgame copies: Arkanoid, Pac-Man, Galaga, Tetris, Lemmings. That much I could have guessed. I asked Armin. «I have absolutely no idea any more where the music came from.» Fair enough, it had been more than twenty years.Then he read a draft about the game, and something clicked: «I’m pretty sure they are all extracts of music from OCRemix.org.»That was the clue. OverClocked ReMix is a huge fan site of video game remixes. I took every remix posted there before the tunes were committed, about 1,200, and slid each loop along them with a spectrum correlation, at a few playback speeds, then checked the hits on the raw waveform. Four of them matched: “Black Block” by DJComet for Arkanoid (played a semitone lower), “64-bit” by Peterrian Productions for Pac-Man, “MkVaffQuasi Ultimix” by MkVaff for Tetris, and “DABOMB” by alk for Lemmings. Every second of each loop scores 0.94 or more against its remix, and under 0.3 against the rest. The script is in the repo, so anyone can check.The Tetris one surprised me. The old README said it was , the Game Boy Tetris. It isn’t. MkVaff’s remix just opens with a Game Boy imitation good enough to fool everybody for twenty years.Galaga was missing. It wasn’t among the remixes OCRemix still publishes, and that turned out to be the hint: the site has withdrawn quite a few remixes over the years. MusicBrainz keeps a list of them, and an old mirror of the removed files survives in the Wayback Machine. In there was “Galagzee” by zee-roh. Waveform correlation 0.98, against 0.014 for a random control. Gone from the site, but the Internet Archive still had it.Red Baron was the one the log already named, but which Red Baron? Not the sequels, and not “Snoopy vs. the Red Baron” either, that one is in another key. A fingerprint search found YouTube recordings of the title music of the 1990 DOS game by Dynamix that clearly matched the tune, but not the recording. So I booted the game in DOSBox with AdLib sound and listened to the title screen. Same melody, same tempo, a different arrangement. Somebody arranged it, and we’ll probably never know who. When I showed Armin, he also thought it might come from that 1990 game.And then there’s ext6, a rock loop for the subgame called Tron, which was later rewritten into a snake game (that name sent me down the wrong path for a while). I searched every OCRemix, current and withdrawn, the old versions on archive.org, the whole VGMix archive, a long list of game music bands from Minibosses to Machinae Supremacy, the music of free games in Debian, Tron soundtracks, Armagetron. Even Shazam. Nothing. If you recognise it, please tell us.OverClocked ReMix only allows unmodified, non-commercial copies, and the other sounds have no known author. So the original tunes and the seven subgame sound effects moved to a folder, and the game got free replacements with the same file names. I picked them by ear, over three rounds, to fit each subgame: CC0 and CC-BY tracks from OpenGameArt by Eric Matyas, HydroGene, Cleyton Kauffman, OwlishMedia and Jonathan Shaw. For Tetris there’s Korobeiniki, the old folk tune, generated by a small script, so it can be rebuilt from source. The sound effects I made from scratch with a little synthesizer script. If the original files are installed the game plays them, and if not it plays the free ones. PROVENANCE.md lists where every file comes from.Everything else has a clear licence. The code is MIT. McSebi’s graphics, sounds, music and levels are under the Artistic License he granted in 2005, in answer to the first ITP. David Gowers put his 2007 graphics under the Artistic License 2.0, and Armin confirmed the Python levels are MIT. That leaves three fan-made level packs with no licence we can find. The Debian package ships only the free part, and a separate package in contrib, bubbros-nonfree-installer (#1153895), downloads the original tunes and those levels for you. If you made one of those level packs, or know who did, please tell us.We need testers. You need Python 3 and pygame ( on Debian):The game opens a control page in your browser. From there you start a game or join one from the Internet list, and the game window opens. Click a dragon, then use the keys for left, right, jump and bubble.bubble.aiei.ch is Alex’s own server, and he plans to keep it running.Tell us what breaks, and on which desktop, in the issues. And if you know your way around Debian, the package is waiting to get back into the archive (ITP #1153735).The control page that opens in your browser.Two players on board 3, on Python 3.An old ITP is a kind of promise, and this one was kept 21 years later. McSebi’s two lines from 2005 are the only reason his graphics can ship in Debian today, so if you write something, say what licence it’s under. The game worked fine on X11 and failed on the desktops people actually use now, and only testing on those desktops showed why. And above all, this is a game made by people. Armin, McSebi, David, Odie, paxed, Gio and Michel-Stéphane made it. Now Alex, anzz1, Christopher Bock and I have picked it up where they left it.If you like this kind of story, Conquer is the long one: a 1987 Usenet game, and twenty years of chasing its authors until it became free software.What game would you bring back, and who would you want to play it with?

item.title: Julian Andres Klode: Introducing apt-core-json
item.author: Julian Andres Klode
item.content:encoded: Today I finalized apt-core-json, the first in a new set of core libraries for APT to bring APT into the new decade, following the latest C++23 standard, with a focus on memory safety, absurd amounts of template metaprogramming, , and of course: coroutines and event loops, leading to a Varlink library as the next big deliverable. The running joke is that the “Core” stands for “outines and vent Loop”.The JSON library was one of the first things needed for a Varlink library. JSON is not particularly hard, but I did not want to write my own parser (and I deleted my old writer!). Instead of a custom library, I had to pick json-c as the backend. I then had to work around a whole ton of issues with json-c not being strict enough; heck that thing will read embedded NUL bytes in strings and then silently truncate them! So we had to implement a verification step that understands enough JSON to reject “\u0000” as well as literal NUL bytes in input strings. In an optimal world, I’d just use sd-varlink, but obviously it’s not available on Hurd.After two loooooooooooong sessions this weekend (10 + 6 hours, and a couple today), this work just landed in main, and I want to share with you the concepts of the library. Very happy to say that this is the first library to have any, let alone , checks.APT::JSON provides two main types:View, which is a read-only view into a JSON objectValue, which is an owned, move-only, mutable referenceLet’s have a look at how this plays out decoding a Varlink call:You may notice the syntax and the call. These are implemented using and templates.Encoders and decoders are relatively straightforward; instantiate the and/or template for the type you want to make encodable, and you are done:Doing this a bunch of times gets old quickly, so of course we added reflection.Reflection allows you to inspect the fields a class has and how they map to JSON keys. Doing so is quite straightforward:But this also gets a bit repetitive so if you want you can use a macro:The macro also takes an optional second argument (a string) to specify the name in the JSON object.One thing to point out is that reflection handles missing fields and null values the same: A is skipped during Encode, and missing fields or values yield equally.The next step is likely , which implements an and utilizing the coroutine features from recent C++ standard versions.Then we can implement and on top of this.The aim is for to likewise be self-describing; a method should have a and an interface an , and the IDL should be automatically generated from it, as well as the dispatch to the coroutines handling responses.This will allow us to have a fully type-safe and exception-free Varlink implementation with incredible ergonomics.

item.title: Maytham Alsudany: Getting your package sponsored in Debian
item.author: Maytham Alsudany
item.content:encoded: Debian packages may seem simple to generate using the many bundling tools out there, but it is much more involved than that. There are policies and procedures in place before stuff can get into Debian, including how the package is made, what it must include, and more. This article aims to cover the stuff prospective contributors to Debian should know that other resources miss.When I started, I didn't know a lot of this and had to learn a lot along the way. Hopefully what I've put together here will make it easier for the next person that comes along.Find the right thing to work onPackages are the bread and butter of Debian, so it may be the first place you look at. There are two ways to go: adopting or helping out with an existing package, or introducing a new package.Outside of packaging, contributing to Debian's infrastructure is also very much welcomed and appreciated, especially as a lot of it is decades old. Some examples include Lintian (Debian package linter), DAK (archive software), and distro-tracker (package info tracker), and there are many, many other projects in need of help.This article mainly focuses on the packaging side of things.Working on an existing packageThe most useful thing you can do as someone interested in packaging is to help with an existing package. You can either:Help other maintainers on an existing package. Maintainers will publish Request for Help (RFH) bugs asking for assistance to maintain a package. Some packages are so unruly that help is welcome even when not asked (e.g. Docker).Adopt an orphaned package. An orphaned package is one where the previous maintainer could not continue maintaining it for whatever reason, and so it needs a new maintainer (or deletion). These are indicated by Orphaned (O) bugs. Request for Adoption (RFA) bugs are similar, as they mean the maintainer is about to orphan the package.Some orphaned packages are effectively abandoned, being both unmaintained upstream and having no users in Debian, but many maintainers will choose to orphan these packages rather than remove them. Keep this in mind when looking through the list.By the way, this is how I started contributing to Debian! With the help of a Debian Developer, I adopted kitty, and to this day I continue to maintain it.Introducing a new packageMany people opt to start their Debian contribution journey through producing a new package for the Debian archive. Unfortunately, many people do not do this properly or try to use Debian as a dumping ground for their own software, so here is a general checklist to see if something belongs in Debian:Repology shows an overview of a package across Linux distributions.How established is the software, and is it still maintained? The longer a project has been around while continuing to be actively maintained, the more likely it is to continue to be maintained in the long-term.How many people use the software? Hundreds? Thousands? How many people will benefit from the software being packaged and included in the Debian archive?The point of packaging something for Debian is to make it easier for the existing userbase to install the software. For instance, as a user you generally expect notable software like Firefox and Vim to be available with a single , and it would be weird if you had to hunt down binary tarballs or build these from source.Do any other Linux distributions package the software? If yes, that's a good indicator it belongs in Debian as well. You can check this on https://repology.org.Does the software introduce new or unique functionality not found in any other software currently present in the archive? It's okay if it doesn't, but there would be a much stronger case for a new package if the answer is yes.Does the software have generally stable releases and proper versioning? If it doesn't, it's going to be a whole lot harder to create and maintain a package for it, considering Debian is a distribution that releases snapshots of software every 1-2 years with nothing but security updates for stable.You also need to keep in mind that you should be prepared to maintain the software throughout the lifetime of the next Debian stable. Debian is not a rolling release distro. You cannot upload new versions of software to stable. The only thing you can upload to stable are fixes that meet the stable release team's criteria, and security fixes via the security archive, which you sometimes have to cherry-pick and backport if upstream does not provide them. And Debian packaging is not a one-off task; you should be ready to look after the package long-term, which consists mostly of updating the package in unstable for new upstream releases and fixing bugs.Many people miss the memo. They bring their "revolutionary" app that they threw together (often vibe-coded) in a weekend and try to get it added to Debian. Project members mostly won't upload such packages; as a result, more useful packages may be drowned out. At the time of writing, I estimate around half of the open Request for Sponsorship (RFS) bugs is this kind of toy software with little to no real users.If you've made something, great! Feel free to package it, but distribute it in your own external repo. Not everything belongs in Debian, and no Debian Developer has an obligation to sponsor and upload your package. Services like GitLab, and Forgejo (Codeberg) also have built-in repository features that let you easily create an external repository.When looking at software that could potentially be packaged, also consider the amount of effort you may have to spend investigating licensing status and compiling copyright information. This is covered a bit later in this article.Now, you probably don't need read the Debian Policy and Debian Developer's Reference from cover to cover, but you should familiarise yourself with Debian packaging and the key infrastructure involved. Look at the important bits in the Policy and Developer's Reference.Look at other similar packages and pay attention to how they were made. Ask questions when you're unsure, people are always willing to answer on the debian-mentors mailing list and IRC channel.Once you get a rough idea of how a Debian package works, it will feel natural working through packaging files.By the way, you can read a lot of these documents offline: manpages can obviously be installed and read on your own machine, but the and packages (from unstable) will allow you to read the policy and reference offline as HTML in their respective directories under /usr/share/doc/.People have many opinions on how to create a package, but by far the most popular is the GBP format for packaging in a git repo.GBP stands for , the tool behind this workflow, based loosely on the DEP-14 proposal. Here, the upstream code is placed in an "upstream" branch (this is what goes in the tarball), and the Debian-specific packaging work is placed in a "debian" branch (this is what goes in the tarball).Many people have different ideas of what these branches should be called: vs , vs vs . It generally doesn't matter though as the end result will be the same either way.Using a git repo for your packaging rather than just a DSC makes it easy to see and review the changes you've made, and allows others to easily get the package source with full history and contribute (when located in a permissive group on Salsa like debian/ or one of the many teams).It goes without saying that you should maintain proper commit hygiene by separating changes into multiple commits, having meaningful commit messages, and avoiding force pushing whenever you can.Commit messages do not need to have explanations like other projects may expect, but feel free to add one if you think it will help whoever is looking at your changes understand what's going on.Keep in mind that you can and should use the gbp-dch-style meta tags, which are , , and , documented in the manpage: will not include your commit in the generated debian/changelog when is executed. will include the extended description of your commit as well in the generated debian/changelog when is executed. will add a thankyou to the person named in the generated debian/changelog when is executed. Useful when a commit is related to a bug report, patch or other useful contribution from someone else. will add the relevant in the generated debian/changelog when is executed, to close one or more (comma-separated) bugs in the Debian Bug Tracker when the package is uploaded.This is the most important one, and should always be used even when not using GBP in an alternative workflow. Most groups on Salsa, including , have webhooks that will send an email to bug reports and tag them as if a commit using this meta tag is pushed, which is great for notifying people that a fix is ready and about to be uploaded.Note: Don't bother trying to add to your "Initial packaging" commit description; there is no need and debian/changelog should already close it in your initial packaging work.More and more packages are being moved into "team" maintenance with weak package ownership, over the traditional single-maintainer model with strong ownership. This allows everyone to help maintain a package through team uploads, rather than relying on the same people to remain active.When it makes sense, you should try to maintain your package in a team, especially as it will have other contributors familiar with the topic or language that may be able to spot issues in your package others may miss.Most packaging teams fit into two categories: - these are teams that package software exclusively written in a specific programming language, and usually also maintain the toolchain for that language as well. Examples include the Go team, Python team, and Rust team. Many of these teams also have their own tooling to make packaging easier for these languages, like and . - these are teams that package software related to a certain topic or project, usually by contributors very interested in that topic. Examples include the Med Team, the Electronics Packaging Team, and the Debian Vim Maintainers.Language-specific libraries like packages should almost always be maintained in a language team, and packages centered around a project like Vim or Treesitter should be put in the related team if it exists. For all other cases, it is completely up to you. It usually does not matter which team you put it in, as long as you put it in team, as you get the same benefits. Keep in mind, many teams have certain policies and guidelines for how packages within them should be maintained, so make sure to check that.If you're maintaining stuff outside of a team, you should consider adding yourself to the LowThresholdNmu list to indicate that you are happy for people to follow a relaxed non-maintainer upload process when it comes to these packages.Upstream sometimes adds files taken from other projects, which must be documented in debian/copyright.Every Debian package must include copyright information. In the packaging source, this is in , and this ends up being installed under /usr/share/doc/<package>/copyright on Debian systems.This is important for a variety of reasons, some of which are:It establishes that the software is compliant with the Debian Free Software Guidelines (when in ).In the case of packages in the and archive areas, it helps people running mirrors or creating installation media (like install USBs) determine which software they are allowed to redistribute.It helps people working in enterprise settings produce a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM).It provides a consistent source of licensing information for software installed on your system so that you, as the end user, don't have to hunt down this information yourself.As a result, this can mean a lot of work hunting down copyright and license information, especially for large software projects. In fact, you will often spend more time on the debian/copyright file than the rest of the package combined when working on Debian packaging.licensecheck - tool to try to detect the license of files passed to itlicenserecon - uses licensecheck to compare detected licenses against those in debian/copyright and shows you the differencesscan-copyrights - generate a preliminary copyright file using licensecheck, useful for finding stuff that got missedWhen the licensing status of a file is unclear, you may have to ask the upstream author to clarify. Note that if something has no license (e.g. upstream does not specify a license at all for their project), it is considered "all rights reserved" and cannot be distributed in Debian.Some projects will have vendored copies of some or all of their dependencies. When this is the case, you need to remove as much as possible and make the package use the libraries provided in Debian instead, as this is a Debian policy requirement (more info on this wiki page on embedded copies). Additionally, you may need to remove non-DFSG-compliant parts of upstream's source to ensure the package is DFSG-free. Both of these are done via repacking, which involves:Specifying the Files-Excluded field in debian/copyright, preferrably with a Comment as well on why it is being repacked.Modifying the tarball retrieved from upstream to remove these files. Some people do this by hand, but it is better to use either (from devscripts) to do this when you already have a tarball, where it will read and use Files-Excluded (refer to it's manpage), or , which will download a new tarball using your debian/watch file and then run on it.Adding a (repackaged for DFSG reasons) or (repackaged to remove vendored copies or other reason) suffix to the upstream version. This will appear in the name of the repackaged tarball (e.g. ), and in the upstream part of the Debian version (e.g. , where is the upstream part). If you end up repacking the same version multiple times, you can add a numeric suffix (e.g. ) to indicate this.Also make sure to check if your package source contains binary files like images and PDFs, and to figure out if they have separate copyright and licensing status. Some of these files have their copyright information embedded within them. Of course, you can ignore build artifacts, as long as they are cleaned and rebuilt during package build.Build and check your packageYou should build your package in a clean unstable environment to ensure that your Build-Depends pull in all the required packages from the unstable repos. The best tool to do this is , which builds your package in an isolated unshare-based environment and allows easily running lintian and autopkgtest as well; this is the same tool used by the Debian build daemons (buildd) once your package is uploaded.There are quality-checking tools available to catch common and not-so-common issues with your packaging. Using the sbuild configuration that the wiki page suggests, after each build it will automatically run:Lintian: static Debian package checker that analyses the outputted files (.deb, .dsc, .changes)Autopkgtest: tests your package as installed on a testbed system if your package defines themPiuparts: checks your package cleanly installs, upgrades and removes (useful for checking custom installation and removal scripts)You should always check the output of these tools and ensure they pass. Debian Developers use these same tools when reviewing your packaging.If you are able to and when it makes sense, you should also install the package onto your own system and check everything works correctly. Even if a package builds successfully, it may not actually work when installed.Unless your package only produces packages, you may want to also check that it cross-compiles correctly. You are probably either reading this on an or device, so you can easily cross-compile to the other architecture using the option with sbuild. Ability to cross-compile is not a policy requirement, but it will be raised as a bug against your package if it fails to do so.Adding on to that, if your package is not straightforward and it produces packages on multiple architectures (usually ), you may want to also check that it compiles on all of Debian's release architectures (aka. official ports). You can do this using virtual machines (QEMU is probably the easiest), but if you can't do this for whatever reason (like your computer being too weak to run a VM or the long package build time), also note that Debian Developers have access to porterbox machines that can be used to check your package before upload.New contributors cannot upload to and manipulate the Debian archive directly. Rather, they need a Debian Developer to do so on their behalf after reviewing all their work; this person is called the "".If you are planning to maintain your package within a team, check if they have their own guidelines or policy for finding a sponsor, as this will likely be quicker than the traditional RFS process outlined below. For instance, in the Go team, sending an email to the mailing list is much better, especially since usually multiple packages need to be uploaded at once.Outside teams, the usual method is to upload your package to mentors.debian.net, and then file a Request For Sponsorship (RFS) bug to ask for a sponsor. The mentors website has an overview and very clear instructions on properly filing an RFS and finding a sponsor.Properly formatted RFS bugs go a long way.When filing the RFS bug, make sure you follow the template exactly. Deviating from it or sending a misformatted email is one of the quickest ways for your RFS to be both ignored by humans and missed by automated tools, so double check that it actually has everything needed. Ensure each of these fields is filled correctly:Package name: This is the name of the source package set in debian/control.Version: The version of the package you want the sponsor to upload, usually the latest version in debian/changelog.Upstream contact: The contact info you put in the field in debian/copyright. This can be a name & email or a URL (e.g. to upstream's issues tracker).URL: The homepage of upstream's website, usually from the field in debian/control.License: List all the licenses present in debian/copyright, comma-separated.Vcs: The URL to your Git repo containing your packaging, which should be on salsa.debian.org and be set up accordingly in the Git-buildpackage format.Section: The value of in debian/control for the source package.Adding notes or comments to the end of the RFS message is fine, but make sure the rest of it follow the right format.Things to keep in mind include:Do not file multiple RFS bugs, for any reason. If you have reuploaded your package or made a change, you can send a follow-up to the same bug.If you want to change the name of your RFS (e.g. following a change in the name of the package), modify the tags or anything else, you can send commands via email to the Bug Tracking System (BTS).Your RFS bug will only be closed if the package is uploaded or someone decides your package should not be uploaded.Do not change the field at the top of the email from , this tells the BTS that your bug report should be filed against and not some package in the archive.The field at the top of the email should be "wishlist" for new packages, "important" for updates fixing Release-Critical (RC) bugs, and "normal" for everything else.Skipping the bug and sending an email directly to the debian-mentors mailing list is a great way for your RFS to be ignored, especially since automated tools will not be able to pick it up.Format the bug's title correctly. It needs to be RFS: name/version [ITP/ITA/RC/NMU] -- short description. Again, this is helpful for automated tools when they try to figure out what your RFS means. Examples include:RFS: qiv/3.0.4-1 [ITA] -- Quick image viewerRFS: wattsi/0.0~git20251112.d8caa36+dfsg-1 [ITP] -- Preprocessor for the HTML StandardNow, when filed properly, an interested sponsor may come along and review your package, then either upload your package or send you feedback to iterate on before that. Ensure you watch for responses to your RFS and respond promptly.Note there is no obligation for anyone to upload your package, and that anyone can review your package but only Debian Developers can upload it for you.The Lintian output given by the Mentors website was usually right, but at the time of writing the website is using an outdated version of Lintian, so many of the hints it gives are incorrect. For the most up-to-date output, it's best to run Lintian from unstable on your own machine (which sbuild does for you).If your package is new to Debian, it will head to the NEW queue for manual review. Here, the DFSG team primarily checks that the package is compliant with the Debian Free Software Guidelines and is suitable for "main", but also check for mistakes in debian/copyright and obvious/major packaging issues.Once your package is uploaded, whether new or existing, and you are named maintainer, you are in charge of looking after it, including new upstream version uploads to unstable, bug fixes, and security fixes. This mostly involves updating and cherry-picking fixes from upstream, but occasionally it gets interesting and you need to dive into the packaging to figure out what's going on and fix the issue.You should try to work towards becoming a Debian Maintainer at the very least in order to easily maintain packages long-term. As a DM, you can be granted upload permissions on a per-package basis for your existing packages so that you don't have to rely on sponsors forever. Having this goal can also appeal to sponsors.(Opinion) What I look for in an RFSThis is not definitive, but I usually scan for these indicators:Upstream and the packager being the same person is usually a red flag for a low-quality package. Exceptions can be made when it makes sense and this would actually be a benefit, but this is rare.Properly formatted BTS bug, which shows ability to follow a simple guide.The software existing in other Linux distros is a good sign.Packaging VCS should be up-to-date, located on Debian Salsa, and follow Git-buildpackage / DEP-14 format. Deviations should only occur for a good reason. Only experienced packagers should really be experimenting with alternative Git styles like dgit-maint-merge etc.I can understand what it does just from the package's full description, without having to go to upstream, since this helps me gauge whether I am interested in sponsoring the package. This is not always the case, since packages sometimes come through of a technical nature (usually kernel-related or maths/science packages) where I wouldn't be able to understand no matter how hard I try.Updates to existing packages and adoptions (ITAs) are easier to sponsor than new packages since it doesn't have to go through the NEW queue and does not need to justify its addition to the archive.Debian Developers and Debian Maintainers speak for themselves, not for the project. They are just people who happen to have some permissions in the project.The only official way to put forward the position of the Debian Project as a whole on a particular issue is through a General Resolution as per Debian's constitution. Other official sources include those maintained by the Publicity Team delegates, such as Debian News and Bits from Debian.Also note that delegates for a certain team can speak on behalf of that team. In this case, they usually get consensus within that team before making such statements.Debian does not have a "legal team", the debian-legal mailing list is for discussion about licensing.There is no "Debian Team", it's just a bunch of contributors working together to deliver a quality collection of packages. Packaging teams are informal, as they are not delegated; rather, they are people working on a certain category of packages under one roof.Keep in mind contributors are all volunteers, with most not getting paid to work on Debian. Debian is owned by a non-profit and relies on donations, rather than a company like Ubuntu and Canonical. The Debian constitution explicitly states that no contributor is obligated to do anything.

item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppArmadillo 15.8.0-1 on CRAN: New Upstream
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: Armadillo is a powerful and expressive C++ template library for linear algebra and scientific computing. It aims towards a good balance between speed and ease of use, has a syntax deliberately close to Matlab, and is useful for algorithm development directly in C++, or quick conversion of research code into production environments. RcppArmadillo integrates this library with the R environment and language–and is widely used by (currently) 1396 other packages on CRAN, downloaded 53.2 million times (per the partial logs from the cloud mirrors of CRAN), and the CSDA paper (preprint / vignette) by Conrad and myself has been cited 743 times according to Google Scholar.This versions updates to the new 15.8.0 upstream Armadillo release made today. As detailed below, it expands the API a little but also updates a few interfaces including one related to sparse matrix operations. As usual, we ran two full reverse-depdency checks against the nearly 1400 packages. This resulted in one additional small change set upstream (and the second reverse-dependency run) along with a small and focusses extension on our side which Kevin very kindly and promptly offered after I was scratching my chin over what may be needed. The package has also already been updated for Debian, built for r2u and should build shortly in r-universe as well as at CRAN for the different binary releases. We also note that we once again had a CRAN: all incoming tests, including full reverse dependencies, passed without the need for a follow-up email and were 100% automated. Smooth sailing!All changes since the last CRAN release follow.Changes in RcppArmadillo version 15.8.0-1 (2026-11-22)Upgraded to Armadillo release 15.8.0 (Medium Roast Chill)Added class for reusing matrix factorisation to solve systems of linear equationsAdded for solving linear least squares with equality constraintsMore efficient handling of Reworked detection of aliasing for cubesAdded support for different sparse matrix expressions (Kevin Ushey in #514 fixing #513)

item.title: Daniel Baumann: Debian: Modernizing iperf/iperf3 and introducing fireperf

item.content:encoded: Recently I spend some time on modernizing the packaging of the Internet Protocol bandwidth measuring tools iperf and iperf3 in Debian, as well as uploading fireperf to Debian.TL;DR: If you want to run your own iperf server,Previously, only built . If you wanted to run an iperf server, you had to do it on your own, i.e. there was no systemd service for that.The package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into and (e.g. when upgrading from to ).For historical reasons, iperf2 is packaged in debian as , not . Now the packages have provides for , , and respectively (so they can be installed by these names too).Updated packages are available in , and backports for are available at Debian Fast Forward.It might make sense in the future…therefore the one is not replacing the other (iperf2 in general is the better tool than iperf3, eventhough the common misconception is that iperf3 is supposedly better than iperf2 because the number 3 is greater than the number 2)…to maybe rename to to match both upstream naming and also to harmonize the packaging of iperf2 with other distributions.TL;DR: If you want to run your own iperf3 server,Previously, only built . If you wanted to run an iperf3 server, had a debconf yes/no question which would then start one iperf3 server on the default port 5201.Since iperf3 (contrary to iperf, also see here and here for iperv vs. iperf3) does not allow using multiple connections on the same port, you have to run multiple iperf3 servers, each on their own port, in order to serve more than one client at the time.The old debconf question for enabling a single iperf3 server has been removed as well as the obsolete sysvinit integration.In order to allow running multiple iperf3 servers at the same time (but on different ports), now contains a systemd service template so you can enable multiple iperf3 servers (e.g. 3 servers on subsequent port numbers, but you can run as many as you want on any ports you like) either manually with:or by using debconf interactively to do it automatically for you (which defaults to one instance on port 5201):or by using debconf non-interactively to do it automatically for you:The package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into and .Updated packages are available in , and backports for are available at Debian Fast Forward.TL;DR: If you want a nicer iperf/iperf3 client,TL;DR: If you want to run your own fireperf server,fireperf is a modern take on the iperf3 network performance and stress-testing tool under the item.title: Russ Allbery: Review: Whalesong
item.author: Russ Allbery
item.content:encoded:
Review: , by Miles Cameron is a far-future semi-military science fiction novel and the third in the Arana Imperii series, not counting the story collection . It did an adequate job of jogging my memory of previous events, but I kind of wish I had re-read the series before reading this entry. and were closely linked, almost one novel in two volumes. is not. There is a frame story featuring Nbaro and Dorcas and an introductory story featuring Nbaro's friend Qaqqaq, but the protagonist for most of the novel is a minor character from the earlier books: Thor Storkel.
After , Storkel mustered out of the DHC and purchased the captured New Texas ship . An arrangement with Morosini involving secret reserve status let him keep a hidden weapon system. His plan was to become an independent trader, working for himself and going wherever he wanted.
This did not go as smoothly has he planned. Keeping a ship running was expensive in numerous ways that had never previously been his problem, and the end of the Non-War meant a glut of ships and crews trying to do the same thing he was doing. His PTSD and associated paranoia from his time on the didn't help. As opens, Storkel is running the by himself (a horrible idea), trying to find both cargo he can make money on and crew he can afford to hire.
Also the antigravity is weirdly glitchy, and he's fairly sure the ship's sub-AI doesn't like him. feels like an interlude in the larger series. Although there are important connections to the larger series plot, the advancement of that plot is limited and mostly happens in the background. Instead, this is more of a merchant adventure with some found family vibes, returning to military SF and larger political concerns only late in the book. It felt like Cameron needed to move pieces into place for the next major plot development and decided to use that interlude to tell a smaller character story.
The appeal of this book is therefore going to depend on how much you like the characters. Storkel is an improviser and a tinkerer, the kind of person who sets up an elaborate set of tools and macros and alarms to partly automate his job without letting go of any piece of it. The primary tension in the story is Storkel's paranoia and the increasing evidence that it is justified, that there is something fundamentally wrong with his ship. By himself, Storkel is a little too intense. Thankfully, he gradually accumulates crew over the course of the story, and that settles him down and adds some enjoyable character interactions. Dorcas, when he shows up, is exactly like Dorcas in the previous books; if you liked him before, you'll still like him here.
This is the kind of book that I enjoyed while reading and then promptly forgot most of as soon as I finished it. The details of Storkel's attempt to become an independent trader and how it is slowly hijacked by the series plot is competent, but not more than that (at least for me). The one real complaint that I have is that Nbaro, even when mostly off-camera, continues to be hypercompetent and central to DHC politics in a way that I found a bit unbelievable. Otherwise, the worst that I can say is that this book never grabbed me like did. I happily turned the pages, but I probably won't read it again.
After reading this book, I re-read both and and greatly enjoyed both of them. I haven't felt any similar desire to re-read this one.
If you're following the series, there's no reason to skip , but I doubt it will be your favorite.
Followed by , which will hopefully have the sort of major plot advancements hinted at by the title. At the time I am writing this review, it is scheduled for publication in September of 2027 in the UK and does not yet have a publishing schedule in the US.

item.title: Matthias Geiger: Using inkscape to draw high-quality electrical diagrams
item.author: Matthias Geiger
item.content:encoded: For my thesis paper I had the need to have high-quality diagrams as images to include in my LaTeX document. While TiKz provides a neat way to do so, sometimes it does not cut it, especially if you want to have a certain degree of flexibility or add some signal forms. Furthermore, writing TikZ (CircuitTikz in this case) can be rather convoluted. While solutions such as the online designer exist, IMO a plain drawing is just better.Fortunately, inkscape has all we need to produce high-quality circuit diagrams. Install it via apt, and then first add the electrical symbols library:git clone https://github.com/upb-lea/Inkscape_electric_Symbols mkdir -p .config/inkscape/symbols cp Inkscape_electric_Symbols/Inkscape_Symbols_all.svg .config/inkscape/symbols Then open inkscape. The newly added symbols can be found at Objects->Symbols (or press CTRL+Shift+Y). To efficiently draw, press "#" to enable the grid, and set "Enable snapping". This makes it easier to align the objects to the grid.Afterwards, one can just drag and drop symbols from the menu onto the drawing area, and construct a transmission line like this:The best part is inkscape also supports plotting signals that follow a mathematical expression. This comes especially in handy if you need to have some signal next to a circuit part. This can be done via Extensions->Render->Function plotter. It is a bit convoluted, since you first need to draw a rectangle, which is then converted to a plot. In this example, I drew a fourier transform of a square wave with five terms:4/pi*(sin(x)+1/3*sin(3*x)+1/5*sin(5*x)+1/7*sin(7*x)+1/9*sin(9*x))Then set some defaults: Check "Remove rectangle"; uncheck "Cut with rectangle", "draw axes" and "Add endpoints on x-axis". For the scaling, I chose an x range of -0.5 to 0.5, checked "multiply x values by 2 pi", an y range of -1 to 1, and 100 data points. I also unchecked isotropic scaling and polar coordinates.The end result (with some inkscape coercing) is a nice jittery rectangluar waveform:Overall, this is pretty nice and allows for high-quality images. Once the svg is finished, it can easily be exported as png. I recommend a DPI of 300.

item.title: Abhijith PA: MiniDebCamp Kochi 2026 - Report

item.content:encoded: On 22nd May 2026, we organized a MiniDebCamp at Bolgatty Palace, Kochi, Kerala.The actual discussion for this year’s camp began when we had a small meetup at Urbec’s place in Kochi. We decided to do a MiniCamp rather than MiniConfs which we were doing for quite some time. Also, We had already done a Bug Squashing Party last year with 4 people and we wanted to do a bigger one this time.Kiran(hacksk) was involved with organizing the camp initially. Later when we finalized the dates for the camp, he had to leave since it conflicted with another event he had to attend. Thanks to Aryan(spaciouscoder) for the event logo and designs. Due to his exam clashes, he also couldn’t attend the event. When Kiran left, AkhilVarkey passionately took the lead in organizing the event. Thanks to him for traveling all the way from his hometown in Thrissur to venue during initial negotiations. In fact, it was only after he joined that the event planning became more systematic, with regular meetings, Kanban boards, spreadsheets, and other tools to keep track of everything. If it had been just me, I would have handled everything as it came up, and things would have been chaotic.Choosing venue wasn’t hard this time. We were already in talk with Bolgatty Palace for a bigger event and we decided to conduct the camp here after couple of visits and negotiations on rates. Our booking was still with them due to the unfortunate event happened during the DebConf23.We opened our registration via LiberaForms as Akhil had decided on avoiding non free platforms for data collection and wanted to do it as private as possible. After exploring our options, we decided on LiberaForms. We prepared a data collection, retention and destruction policy for the event. We purposefully only asked for the required fields. We were so particular that we didn’t even have a phone number field but this backfired a little. Turns out many people don’t check mail as frequent as we thought. Inspite of it, we managed to reach out with updates on the event successfully.In parallel, we also sent out some mails for sponsorships. Thanks to OnlyOffice and FOSSUNITED who generously sponsored our event and enabled us to accommodate more participants. Since its a camp and not just a BSP like last year, we welcomed new people to the event.We started the event on Friday evening. We did a small orientation for new comers. Before the event, we shortlisted some bugs and tasks to share. All began hacking on stuffs that was interesting to them. Some did packaging, some did bug fixes and others worked on website fixes. There was even some fiddling done on beagleboard SBC and other boards.The venue was calm and serene. The weather was nice, notwithstanding the few downpours we experienced. Some people from Hyderabad (South eastern side) and Kolkata actually got amazed by the tropical greenery around the venue and Kochi in general. The food served to us through out the event was amazing and accommodation was also very nice.In terms of bug squashing statistics, we managed to touch 93 bugs \o/ and of which 82 bugs are resolved. Parallel to bug squashing, Subin (bin/su) and Muneer worked on revamping the Debian Project website. MRs . Akhil worked on KDE things. One among is angelfishSeeing the outcome, we are hopeful and thrilled to conduct this as an annual event. Couple of people had a brainstorm later and the current decision is to do similar event next year in Bengaluru, given it will be more accessible than Kochi.Akhil had been nudging me to finish this report for the umpteenth time, and it’s finally published. (Thanks for the proof read also, which you have done months back)

item.title: Russell Coker: WordPress Content Security Policies
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded: As I already had the Apache module installed I should have been able to set the policy with the following in /etc/wordpress/htaccess:Header set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'"I used the program from the Debian package to see the headers that were being set and that wasn’t in it. I don’t know why it didn’t work and would appreciate any comments making suggestions. I’m not particularly bothered about this as I found a solution that is better for my needs, but the top Google results weren’t helpful and it would be good if the information was out there if anyone already knows how to solve this.To set the header I put the following in /etc/wordpress/config-etbe.coker.com.au.php:header("Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'");I tested that with the command and it was set. I tested it by loading a blog post that had images sourced from www.coker.com.au and the images weren’t loaded according to the policy.So then I changed the line in the configuration file to the following and it worked and allowed my images.header("Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' www.coker.com.au secure.gravatar.com");find /usr/share/wordpress/wp-content -name "*.js"|wc -lCurrently on my blog server the above command shows that there are 1299 Javascript files included in themes and plugins. If one of them has hostile code then it can just run things in the browser when someone visits my site. So if a hostile party gains access to release an update to one of the plugins or themes and I install the update then the code runs.A hostile party wants their code to be concealed and putting a large piece of malware in a package will be easier to spot. Also Krebs documented the malware authors as running A/B tests which also requires taking code from outside sources.The Content-Security-Policy header doesn’t stop hostile code being run if it was installed on the server but it does prevent that code from calling out to other code from other servers. This means that it will be harder for attackers to hide code which is a benefit for defenders. If an attacker aims for the common case of this header not being used then their malware will work on most sites but not on mine which is a win for me. When protecting against large scale attacks you often only need to be slightly more secure than most sites.If most sites do this then attackers will include all the malware inline which means that my site will be vulnerable but also means that the malware will be easier to spot. So that is still a win for defenders.I don’t think I have completely solved a problem, but I think I have improved things and that others will benefit from doing the same thing.The site securityheaders.com [3] is of a similar nature to the more well known ssltest [4] site. According to securityheaders.com my site only gets a “C” rating so there’s work to do there.Is there a good way of using free software to automatically check Javascript for hostile code? A google search has turned up a few options but it will take some time to investigate them even after ruling one out for being non-free.

item.title: Matthias Klumpp: Changes on freedesktop.org!
item.author: Matthias
item.content:encoded: You can read the announcement here, this blog post elaborates a bit on it and on the background of the changes, as well as future plans.The freedesktop.org website has been a wiki for a long time, which definitely was the right call in its inception. A wiki is very much in spirit of Freedesktop’s mission statement to foster collaboration between desktop environments and to be a place to create de-facto standards.However, over the years, working with the wiki became a bit of an issue: Not only did we face multiple spam-apocalypses (which in part motivated the switch to IkiWiki in 2013 and resulted in us heavily restricting write access to the wiki), but it also meant that official project information, finished specifications, half-finished proposals and pages nobody had touched in fifteen years were all sitting next to each other.Since 2000 when Freedesktop.org was started, the project has grown so much and has had so many associated projects and specifications over the decades that it is now very difficult for new people to get an overview what is current and what state the software projects and specifications hosted by Freedesktop.org are in.Having only a wiki as a large and somewhat disorganized pile of information did not help with that issue, so I worked to split things up: We now have a website as well as a wiki, using different designs to distinguish the two, and serving different purposes.The website at www.freedesktop.org will be the place for “official”, or rather, more curated information. Now that the new website is live, its content is still largely that of the old wiki. Over the next weeks, I will be working on cleaning up its contents and listings. For example, I will clearly split active projects from archived ones, add missing ones, and also work towards synchronizing the specifications hosted on the former wiki / website with the ones listed on specifications.fd.o.So, basically I will do an inventory check of Freedesktop. That work has already started, but until now, I could not make any public changes to not disrupt workflows or make my own future work harder by having diverging information in two places (website & wiki).I also wanted to make it easier for people to find information on how to get involved with Freedesktop and associated projects, so the new website now has a more discoverable section for that.Of course, we also still want to keep the Wiki and all of its rich history around! It remains the easy-to-edit place for collaboration on upcoming projects and specifications.Wiki edits must now happen through GitLab instead of the old IkiWiki web interface. While this sounds like an additional barrier to edit the wiki, it is significantly easier than requesting an account on to edit the old Wiki through the web interface. It also still allows us to keep the existing history as well as spam protection measures. In order to use the wiki with GitLab Pages and to keep the history easily accessible and readable, I rewrote the Git history of the wiki to make it pretend that all changes always happened in a subdirectory. So, if commit signatures are missing and hashes are different: That is the only reason why. There have been no content changes or other metadata changes (and we still have a copy of the pristine wiki Git repository).For the fd.o wiki, we are now also using Hari’s IkiWiki template that is already in use on the X.org website and which is much easier on the eyes.At the moment, I am mostly concerned with ensuring that the change has not broken any existing links and all systems keep working. After that, the wiki 🡘 website deduplication work will start and we can modernize both the content of the website and wiki.If you find a broken link, an outdated page or anything else that looks wrong, please file an issue or, even better, open a merge request.For the wiki, you are very welcome to just fix or otherwise update the page directly.I did reach out to all wiki editors and projects impacted by this change in advance, but since there are so many people and projects involved, it is always possible to miss someone or something. If you found a bug, need edit permissions, or need help with anything, don’t hesitate to ping me: You can find me as in OFTC’s IRC channel, in the very recently created #xdg-specs channel on the Freedesktop Matrix space, or you can email me.I do want to echo the announcement news post here: None of Freedesktop.org would exist without the people who filled it with life over the years and who worked on cross-desktop collaborative projects. I have read through a lot of wiki history and old project pages over the recent months, and it feels amazing to know how much work and passion people have poured into the projects and collaborative efforts over the years – no matter if they were successes in the end, or remained experiments. I am very thankful for all current, past and future editors of the website and wiki, as well as all project maintainers and contributors.Thanks to all contributors, in whichever way you contribute to our free desktop ecosystem!

item.title: Francesco Paolo Lovergine: Terramaster NASes with Debian, take three: scaling up.
item.author: Francesco P. Lovergine
item.content:encoded: As is often the case in scientific environments, IT solutions grow chaotically, often guided by available funds at the wrong moments, or transient choices for transient goals. Here at work, we are not an exception. Historically, since the birth of the Copernicus European project, the Earth Observation domain has become progressively more demanding about storage, due to the frequency and size of satellite acquisitions, available free of charge for research groups, free to access, but not without maintenance and processing costs, of course.As a result, we have progressively explored low-cost solutions for downloading and processing Sentinel constellation time series. Over a ten-year window, our needs moved from dozens of terabytes to hundreds of terabytes. We started with simple Synology-based solutions, very optimistically, only to discover that the optimism was not justified. When storage needs to scale up, there are no easy solutions.The only comparable IT environments are HPC clusters, which operate at a completely different order of magnitude in terms of funding. In that context, the Petabyte order of magnitude is generally achievable by using proprietary/FOSS distributed POSIX filesystems such as GPFS, Lustre, or even Ceph. None of them are exempt from problems from time to time. The sad reality is that maintaining a very large POSIX filesystem requires compromises, and no single solution fits all requirements, starting from cost to flexibility, scalability, and reliability. I wrote about the hidden costs of maintaining self-hosted storage solutions hereAlmost ten years ago, we chose GlusterFS as an acceptable compromise for a distributed POSIX filesystem. It is not object storage, but a pure POSIX filesystem with a simple architecture, which fits our environment, where most people rely on the folders-and-files abstraction to organize their data. All nodes and their bricks are equal (no dedicated metadata nodes) and can scale without major limitations with a reasonable number of nodes. In our experience, the real bottleneck is network speed, which can introduce high latency and cause cache issues.We are now finally moving our old Synology-based distributed filesystem to a pool of TerraMaster U12-500 Plus units, installed with Debian 13. Compared with TerraMaster SOHO products, these rack-mount units can run without any non-free firmware. You must manually enable the usual 9000 MTU jumbo frame for the 10Gb network, which is generally required on all connected hosts and also the switch (in our case, a MikroTik box) to properly manage full bandwidth. We measured average performance around 200MB/sec, which aligns with the average sequential speed of 6Gb SATA HDDs.Regarding using GlusterFS, the most obvious choice is to use it with XFS as the filesystem for the NAS bricks; this proved in practice to be the optimal configuration, after not-too-nice experiences with Btrfs on Synology DSM. Still, it requires some tuning for periodic checks across the various layers of the storage system. One is about short/long HDD testing, which I already covered in another post. A trickier aspect is managing possible bit rot in the brick filesystems from time to time. While Btrfs, with its COW management, can run low-impact scrubs on both metadata and data, XFS can only partially do the same for metadata through xfs_scrub, which is also, as clearly stated, an experimental feature to use at your own risk. In that regard, it is much better to run GlusterFS scrubbing instead.While xfs_scrub is as light as the SMART short self-test for HDDs, both RAID checks and GlusterFS bitrot scrub are heavy operations that should run rarely to avoid stressing HDDs and systems, and never at the same time. It is mandatory to avoid overlapping all such operations, and that’s a good reason to use systemd timers and run the heavy checks in alternating months.One suboptimal aspect of our solution is the absence of direct LED control for HDDs, which is unfortunately available only under TOS with a proprietary driver. This is obviously required for disk replacement from time to time, when needed. On the other hand, software support is extended to the lifetime of the Debian distribution, with major upgrades every 3-4 years on average. Also, this is much more flexible and efficient than using pre-built custom OSes. Of course, if you prefer dashboards and the usual GUI candy, this isn't a viable choice; a better option would be TrueNAS, which has a much higher memory footprint, especially when paired with OpenZFS.

item.title: John Goerzen: What is this AI slop bug report trying to achieve?
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: This morning, I opened up my inbox to find a report of a security bug in C-Kermit. “That’s great!”, I thought. Someone else interested in C-Kermit found a bug.Well, as you can imagine from the title of this post, that’s not the case at all.The bug report claimed that a recent security fix was incomplete for non-Unix platforms. It appeared to quote code that lacked hardening. However, the report had the hardening code from the section it quoted. Its suggested fix asked for hardening code… of the exact same shape that is already in the tree, that the report had somehow excluded. Even if the hardening was omitted, from my understanding, the one non-Unix platform that people build C-Kermit on today, OpenVMS, doesn’t have the same class of shell bugs that Unix does.So, the entire report was bunk. It bears every indication of being AI-generated. It arrived in an email with a plain text body, but was formatted Markdown. The writing bore many hallmarks of being AI generated.But it left me wondering: what is this person trying to achieve?And this is a bit of a mystery to me. The email I received concluded with:I'd be grateful if you could: 1. confirm and fix this, 2. publish a GHSA and request a CVE ID, 3. credit "[REDACTED]" as the reporter.I wonder what the end game is?Incidentally, there was no real name used in the report. Only a github username, which I am redacting in this post.It gets stranger. That person on Github appears to have a 3-year-old account, dormant until today, and created a bunch of repos consisting of logs of submitting reports to projects — all of which happened today.Stranger, each of these repos contains enough information in the title for people to pretty much figure out what the bug is (if any of them are reporting actual bugs). Yet they claim to be a “coordinated disclosure” when all of this is public. (I got a more detailed report by email). If any of these are real bugs, this public exposure before a fix opens them up to harm. Their username is plastered all over things in unnecessary places: the report file, the description of the repo, etc.So, what is the point of all this? I don’t get it. They targeted a bunch of, frankly rather obscure, projects with low effort, but with evidence of scripting in the Github interactions. Even if they had an LLM do all this for them… why? I don’t get it.: I replied to the reporter’s email, calling out the problems with it and calling it AI slop. I received a reply, which was extremely obviously AI written, apologizing profusely and claiming that the original had not been written by an AI. Also, all the repos that were on the account yesterday are gone today. I wonder how many times this pattern has repeated over the last 3 years.
